不丹.note:
Capital: Punakha (winter capital)
Polity: Wangchuck dynasty; Ugyen Wangchuck was elected first hereditary king in 1907
Key events: under the Treaty of Punakha of January 1910 Britain undertook not to interfere in its internal affairs, Bhutan accepted British guidance in its external relations, and its annual subsidy was raised to 100,000 rupees; under the treaty with India of August 1949 its external relations came under Indian guidance instead, and India returned a small piece of land at Dewangiri.

东北抗日义勇军.note: Anti-Japanese forces organized spontaneously after the September 18 Incident by patriotic officers and soldiers and people of all strata in the Northeast, nominally under Zhang Xueliang and the Nationalist Government. In 1932 Li Du and Ding Chao's Jilin Self-Defence Army held Yilan, Wang Delin's National Salvation Army held Ning'an and Dunhua, Ma Zhanshan rose again at Heihe in April, and Su Bingwen took up arms at Hailar in September. From the end of the year to early 1933 they were defeated one after another; the main forces withdrew into the Soviet Union, while the rest kept up guerrilla warfare.

东北抗联.note: The anti-Japanese armed forces of the Northeast led by the Communist Party of China. The CPC-led anti-Japanese guerrilla units across the Northeast were organized as the Northeast People's Revolutionary Army after 1933, and in February 1936 uniformly renamed the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, eventually forming eleven armies grouped into the First Route Army (Yang Jingyu, southern Northeast China and the Changbai Mountains), the Second Route Army (Zhou Baozhong, eastern Jilin) and the Third Route Army (Li Zhaolin, northern Northeast China and the Lesser Xing'an Mountains). After 1938 the Japanese and puppet “punitive expeditions” intensified; Yang Jingyu gave his life in 1940, and in 1940–1941 the remaining forces withdrew into the Soviet Union, where they were trained as the Training Brigade, returning to the Northeast in coordination with the Soviet army in 1945. The Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army persisted in the War of Resistance for fourteen years under extremely harsh conditions.

东北解放区.note: From September 1945 the CPC sent more than 100,000 troops and large numbers of cadres into the Northeast, first called the Northeast People's Autonomous Army and renamed the Northeast Democratic Allied Army in January 1946; after Soviet troops withdrew they moved into Harbin and other cities in northern Northeast China and built up the Northeast base area. After the three crossings south of the Songhua and four defences of Linjiang and the summer, autumn and winter offensives, the Liaoshen Campaign ended in victory in November 1948 and the whole of the Northeast was liberated; in August 1949 the Northeast People's Government (Gao Gang) was set up, based at Shenyang. In 1949–1954 it governed the six provinces of Liaodong, Liaoxi, Jilin, Songjiang, Heilongjiang and Rehe and the cities of Shenyang, Lüda and others; in November 1952 it became the Northeast Administrative Committee, which was abolished in June 1954, Liaodong and Liaoxi being merged into Liaoning and Songjiang into Heilongjiang.

东印度尼西亚邦.note: Set up with Dutch backing in December 1946 after the Denpasar Conference on Bali; it covered Celebes, the Moluccas and the Lesser Sunda Islands, with its capital at Makassar, and was the largest “autonomous state” in the Indonesian federation the Netherlands envisaged, intended to divide the Republic of Indonesia. It joined the Republic of the United States of Indonesia in December 1949 and was merged into the unitary Republic of Indonesia in August 1950.

东孟加拉.note: In October 1905 Curzon partitioned Bengal, forming a province from the Dacca, Chittagong and Rajshahi divisions together with Assam, with its capital at Dacca and a Muslim majority. The Indian people's anti-partition movement forced the British King to announce its reversal at the Delhi Durbar of 1911, and in April 1912 it was merged back into Bengal.

东江纵队.note: An anti-Japanese guerrilla force of the people of Guangdong led by the Communist Party of China, with Zeng Sheng as commander. It grew in 1938 out of anti-Japanese armed groups in Huiyang, Bao'an and Dongguan; after Hong Kong fell at the end of 1941, it rescued cultural figures stranded in Hong Kong and Allied personnel, and formed the Hong Kong–Kowloon Independent Brigade. The Dongjiang Column was formally established at Tuyang in Huiyang in December 1943, based at Dalingshan in Dongguan, Yangtaishan in Bao'an and the Dapeng Peninsula; by the end of the War of Resistance it had grown to more than 10,000 men, operating along both banks of the Dong River, and was an important force in the resistance behind enemy lines in South China.

东突厥斯坦伊斯兰共和国.note:
A separatist regime set up by a handful of separatists in southern Xinjiang, the so-called “Islamic Republic of East Turkestan”.
Seat: Kashi (1933.11–1934.02)
Polity: self-styled Islamic republic, with Khoja Niyaz as “president” (he never took up the post) and Sabit Damolla as “prime minister”.
Key figures: Muhammad Amin Bughra (Hotan), Sabit Damolla, Khoja Niyaz.
Key events: in spring 1933 rebellions broke out one after another in Hotan, Kuqa and elsewhere; the regime was proclaimed at Kashi on 12 November, advocating separatism and seeking recognition from Britain and Afghanistan, but was recognized by no country. In February 1934 the Dungan army of Ma Zhongying's forces took the old city of Kashi; its ringleaders fled to Yengisar and Hotan, Khoja Niyaz went over to Sheng Shicai, and the remnants collapsed one after another between April and July.

东突厥斯坦共和国.note:
The Three Districts Revolutionary Government, based at Yining. In November 1944 the people of all ethnic groups in Ili rose against the reactionary rule of the KMT and, with Soviet support, launched the Yining Uprising; the Three Districts Revolution broke out, part of China's New Democratic Revolution. In the early stage of the uprising the leadership was for a time controlled by separatists such as Alikhan Töre, who set up the so-called “Republic of East Turkestan”.
In April 1945 it formed the National Army, which took control of the three districts of Ili, Tacheng and Ashan one after another and in September reached the Manas River, threatening Dihua.
After the Sino-Soviet treaty was signed the Soviet Union urged a ceasefire; from October it held peace talks with the Nationalist Government's representative Zhang Zhizhong, and in January 1946 the peace terms were signed. In June the provisional government was abolished and reorganized as the Ili Special District, joining the Xinjiang provincial coalition government; the three districts nonetheless remained a self-contained entity, and were merged with the rest of Xinjiang on its peaceful liberation in 1949.

中共.note:
The Communist Party of China, founded in Shanghai in July 1921; on the map its units are the armed forces and governments it led.
In 1924–1927 it brought about the first KMT–CPC cooperation, driving forward the Great Revolution and the Northern Expedition; after the failure of the Great Revolution it launched the Nanchang Uprising, the Autumn Harvest Uprising and the Guangzhou Uprising, created the people's army, and established revolutionary base areas in the countryside such as Jinggangshan, the Central, the Hubei-Henan-Anhui and the Western Hunan-Hubei base areas, taking the road of the armed independent regime of workers and peasants.
In November 1931 the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established at Ruijin, with Mao Zedong as chairman. After the failure of the fifth counter-“encirclement” campaign in 1934 the Red Army set out on the Long March; the Zunyi Meeting was held in January 1935, and the Central Red Army reached northern Shaanxi in October.
With the second KMT–CPC cooperation in 1937 the Red Army was reorganized as the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army, which opened up the battlefield behind enemy lines and built border regions and anti-Japanese base areas in Northwest, North and Central China such as Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia and Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei; by 1945 the areas under its administration had a population of nearly 100 million.
In 1946 the KMT launched a full-scale civil war; the People's Liberation Army fought the three great campaigns of Liaoshen, Huaihai and Pingjin and the Yangtze River Crossing Campaign of April 1949, and on 1 October the People's Republic of China was founded. In 1950 Hainan Island and Zhoushan were liberated, and in October the Chinese People's Volunteers entered Korea to resist US aggression and aid Korea.
Key figures: Chen Duxiu, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi.

中华革命军东北军.n: Northeast Army of the Chinese Revolutionary Army (Ju Zheng)
中华革命军东北军.note: An anti-Yuan army organized in Shandong by the Chinese Revolutionary Party under Sun Yat-sen, with Ju Zheng as commander-in-chief and Japanese-occupied Qingdao as its rear base. In May 1916 it took Weixian, Zhoucun and other places; after Yuan Shikai's death it was reorganized and disbanded.

中印度.note: The Central India Agency and the Gwalior Residency: Indore (Holkar family), Gwalior (Scindia family), Bhopal, Rewa and other princely states. They joined India in 1947 and the following year were combined into Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh and other unions.

中原解放区.note: Originally Li Xiannian's Central Plains Military Region; in June 1946 KMT forces besieged it in strength, the Central Plains Military Region forces broke out, and most of the Liberated Area was lost. It was rebuilt in 1947 after the Liu-Deng Army thrust into the Dabie Mountains, the Chen-Xie Group thrust into western Henan and the Chen-Su Army entered the Henan-Anhui-Jiangsu region; the Central Plains Bureau was set up in May 1948 and the Central Plains Provisional People's Government (Kaifeng) in March 1949. Following the Fourth Field Army south, it extended to Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi, Guangdong and Guangxi; in February 1950 the Central-South Military and Administrative Committee (Lin Biao) was set up, seated at Wuhan. In November 1952 it became the Central-South Administrative Committee, and on the abolition of Pingyuan Province the Xinxiang, Anyang and Puyang area went to Henan; it was abolished in 1954.

中圻.note: A protectorate under the Nguyễn dynasty, with the emperor at Huế and real power in the hands of the French Résident supérieur. In March 1945 the Japanese had Bảo Đại proclaim “independence”, creating the Empire of Vietnam; Bảo Đại abdicated on 30 August. Throughout the War of Resistance against France the Quảng Ngãi–Bình Định area remained the Viet Minh's Interzone V. From 1949 it formed Central Vietnam within the State of Vietnam; the 1954 Geneva Accords made the Bến Hải River near the 17th parallel the provisional military demarcation line, with the area north of it going to the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

中央.note: Chiang Kai-shek's own Whampoa clique troops (the Central Army) and the areas directly controlled by the Nanjing Nationalist Government. Built around the First Army during the Northern Expedition, after 1927 it held rich provinces such as Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Shanghai, Anhui, Jiangxi and Fujian; in the wars among the new warlords it defeated the Guangxi Clique, Feng Yuxiang and Yan Xishan in turn, gaining control of Hunan, Hubei, Henan and Shandong, and directed the successive “encirclement” campaigns against the revolutionary base areas; in the later part of the War of Resistance it governed most of the Southwest and Northwest.

中央直辖.n: Provinces and municipalities under the central government
中央直辖.note: In June 1954 the Central People's Government Council decided to abolish the administrative committees of the six greater administrative regions (Northeast, North China, East China, Central-South, Northwest and Southwest), which was completed by the end of the year, and all provinces and municipalities came directly under the central government; in September the First National People's Congress adopted the Constitution of the People's Republic of China, and the Central People's Government was replaced by the State Council. At the same time several provinces were merged: Liaodong and Liaoxi into Liaoning, Songjiang into Heilongjiang, and Ningxia into Gansu; Suiyuan Province had already been merged into the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The map shows the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region and the Local Government of Xizang separately; Xinjiang became the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in 1955, and the provinces of Rehe and Xikang were abolished in 1955.

中央省.note: Capital at Nagpur. Berar nominally belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad but was leased to Britain in perpetuity from 1903, and from 1936 the two were officially styled together as the Central Provinces and Berar. It went to India in 1947.

中央红军.note: The main force of the Red First Front Army, which was forced to leave the Central Soviet Area in October 1934 and began the Long March; it built no base areas on the march, only holding towns temporarily as it passed. It joined forces with the Red Fourth Front Army at Maogong in June 1935, was reorganized as the Shaanxi-Gansu Detachment in September, reached northern Shaanxi in October, and resumed the designation Red First Front Army in November.

中央苏区.note: The Central Revolutionary Base Area, the base area in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian centred on Ruijin. In 1929 the Red Fourth Army came down from Jinggangshan and fought its way through southern Jiangxi and western Fujian; by 1930 the Southwestern Jiangxi and Western Fujian soviet areas had formed, and in 1931, after defeating three “encirclement” campaigns in succession, they were joined into one; in November the Chinese Soviet Republic made Ruijin its capital. At its height it covered more than twenty counties; after the failure of the fifth counter-“encirclement” campaign in 1934 the Central Red Army was forced to withdraw and began the Long March.

也门.note:
Capital: Sanaa
Polity: the Mutawakkilite Kingdom founded by the Zaydi Imam Yahya (1904–1948)
Key events: by the Treaty of Daan of 1911 the Ottomans recognized its autonomy in the Zaydi highlands; independent after the Ottoman withdrawal in 1918, it took over Sanaa and Taiz, and took Hodeidah in 1925; in 1919–1928 it sent troops into the northern Aden Protectorate but was driven back by British air raids; defeated in the Saudi–Yemeni War of 1934, it recognized Saudi sovereignty over Asir, Jizan and Najran in the Treaty of Taif; Yahya was assassinated in February 1948, and his son Ahmad put down the revolt and succeeded him.

井岳秀.note: Jing Yuexiu, Garrison Commissioner of Northern Shaanxi, based at Yulin, held the twenty-three counties of northern Shaanxi as his own domain for nearly twenty years from 1917; the Beiyang Government, the Guominjun and the Nanjing Nationalist Government each confirmed him in office in turn, but real power never changed hands. His subordinate Gao Shuangcheng, stationed at Yan'an, later became the main adversary of the Red Army in northern Shaanxi.

亚丁.note: Occupied by Britain in 1839 and attached to the Bombay Presidency of British India, it was a coaling port on the Suez–India route; separated from India on 1 April 1937, it became a Crown colony.

亚丁保护地.note: The tribal sheikhdoms of the Aden hinterland such as Lahej and Dhala (the Western Aden Protectorate) and the Qu'aiti and Kathiri sultanates of Hadhramaut and the Mahra Sultanate (the Eastern Aden Protectorate), supervised by British advisers. In the First World War Ottoman troops held Lahej until the end of 1918; in 1919–1928 the Yemeni Imam's forces occupied the north.

亚美尼亚.note:
Capital: Erivan
Polity: republic established on 28 May 1918, governed by the Dashnak party
Key events: halted the Ottoman army at the Battle of Sardarabad in May; disputed territory with Georgia and Azerbaijan in 1918–1920, taking over Kars in 1919; lost Kars in the Turkish–Armenian War of September–December 1920 and was Sovietized in December; Zangezur held out until July 1921; joined the Transcaucasian Federation in 1922 and became a union republic in 1936.

人民军占领区.note: On 25 June 1950 the Korean People's Army crossed the 38th parallel, took Seoul on the 28th, swept through the southwestern provinces in late July and reached the Nakdong River in early August; the whole South except the Busan Perimeter was occupied, and people's committees were set up and land reform carried out. After the US Incheon landing in September it was forced to withdraw north. In January 1951, in the Third Campaign, the Chinese People's Volunteers and the Korean People's Army again took Seoul and the area down to the 37th parallel (shown on the map as the “Chinese and Korean forces–held area”), withdrawing in March; thereafter only the Kaesong, Ongjin and Yonan area south of the 38th parallel remained, which became part of the DPRK after the armistice.

以色列.note:
Capital: Tel Aviv; from December 1949 West Jerusalem was made the capital
Polity: parliamentary democratic republic
Key figures: Ben-Gurion (prime minister), Weizmann (president)
Key events: the state was proclaimed on 14 May 1948, before the British mandate ended; the next day Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon sent in troops, and the first Middle East war broke out; after two truces and counter-offensives Israel controlled about 78% of the former mandate territory; in February–July 1949 it signed separate armistice agreements with four neighbouring states; more than 700,000 Palestinian Arabs became refugees.

伊拉克.note:
Capital: Baghdad
Polity: British forces gradually occupied Mesopotamia in 1914–1918; the San Remo Conference of April 1920 made it a British mandate; Faisal I was enthroned on 23 August 1921, and it became a constitutional monarchy under the Hashemite dynasty
Key events: the great revolt against the British in 1920; the status of Mosul settled in 1926; independence and admission to the League of Nations on 3 October 1932; Rashid Ali's coup in April 1941, after which, following the Anglo-Iraqi War of May, British troops were stationed there again; sent troops into Palestine in 1948.

伊朗.note:
Capital: Tehran
Polity: constitutional monarchy under the Qajar dynasty (constitution of 1906); in December 1925 Reza Khan ascended the throne, founding the Pahlavi dynasty
Key events: the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 divided its north and south into spheres of influence; in 1911 tsarist Russia by ultimatum forced out the American financial adviser Shuster and had the Majlis dissolved; though it declared neutrality in the First World War, it was overrun in turn by Russian, British and Ottoman troops; Reza Khan's coup in February 1921; from March 1935 it used the name “Iran” internationally; in August 1941 Britain and the Soviet Union sent in troops and occupied it, Reza Shah abdicated and his son Mohammad Reza succeeded; the Azerbaijan crisis of 1946; the nationalization of oil in March 1951 recovered sovereignty over its oil, and in April Mosaddegh became prime minister; in August 1953 the United States and Britain engineered a coup that overthrew the Mosaddegh government and the Shah took personal rule, and in 1954 an agreement with an international oil consortium resumed exports.

伊沙拉.note:
Capital: Vientiane
Polity: independence-movement government led by Prince Phetsarath
Proclaimed Laotian independence in Vientiane on 12 October 1945 and for a time deposed King Sisavang Vong. In March–May 1946 French troops reoccupied Thakhek, Vientiane and Luang Prabang from south to north, and the government went into exile in Thailand; it dissolved in 1949, and Souphanouvong separately joined with the Viet Minh to form the Pathet Lao front.

伪满洲国.note:
Capital: “Xinjing” (Changchun) (1932.03–1945.08)
Polity: a puppet regime backed by Japanese imperialism; in 1932 Puyi became “Chief Executive” with the reign title Datong; in March 1934 it became a monarchy, styled the “Empire of Manchukuo”, with the reign title Kangde. The director of the General Affairs Agency and the vice-ministers of all ministries were Japanese, and real power lay with the commander of the Kwantung Army.
Territory: the occupied three northeastern provinces, with Rehe annexed in 1933 and the Puppet Xing'an provinces set up separately; the Kwantung Leased Territory and the South Manchuria Railway Zone remained Japanese. Through it Japan exercised colonial rule over the Northeast.
Key events: the Japan–Manchukuo Protocol of 1932; in 1935 the Soviet Union sold the Chinese Eastern Railway to Puppet Manchukuo; Japan pursued a plan to settle a million households of “pioneer groups” in the Northeast; the Battle of Nomonhan in 1939; in August 1945 the Soviet Red Army entered the Northeast, Puyi announced his abdication at Dalizigou, and Puppet Manchukuo collapsed.

俄国.note:
Capital: St Petersburg (renamed Petrograd in 1914) → Moscow (from March 1918)
Polity: Russian Empire (tsarist autocracy) → February Revolution of March 1917, Provisional Government → October Revolution of November 1917, the Bolsheviks establish Soviet Russia → Soviet Union founded on 30 December 1922
Key figures: Nicholas II, Kerensky, Lenin, Trotsky, Stalin
In Asia: the Trans-Siberian Railway and the Chinese Eastern Railway extended Russian power into China's Northeast and Outer Mongolia. During the Civil War and foreign armed intervention of 1918–1922, Siberia was held in turn by the Czechoslovak Legion, Kolchak, Semyonov and the Japanese forces, and Soviet Russia gradually recovered the Far East, using the Far Eastern Republic as a buffer. In 1921 it sent troops into Outer Mongolia and instigated its “independence”, and in 1924 the Mongolian People's Republic was established; the Chinese Eastern Railway Incident in 1929; in 1937 it forcibly deported the Koreans of the Far East to Central Asia; in 1938–1939 it fought Japanese forces at Zhanggufeng and Nomonhan, and in 1941 concluded the Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact. In August 1945 it declared war on Japan and sent troops into China's Northeast, northern Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and after the war divided Korea with the United States along the 38th parallel. On 14 February 1950 it signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance with the People's Republic of China, and during the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea aided China and Korea with munitions and air force units; at the end of 1952 it handed the Chinese Changchun Railway over to China; Stalin died in March 1953, and during Khrushchev's visit to China in October 1954 it agreed to return the Lüshun naval base to China the following year.

信德.note: Conquered by British force in 1843 and long part of the Bombay Presidency; made a separate province on 1 April 1936, with its capital at Karachi. It went to Pakistan in 1947, and Karachi became Pakistan's capital.

俾路支.note: British Baluchistan (Quetta-Pishin, Chagai and other districts) and the Baluchistan Agency, with the Chief Commissioner at Quetta, commanding the Bolan Pass and the railway to the frontier towards Kandahar. A great earthquake struck Quetta in May 1935. It went to Pakistan in 1947.

傅作义.note: A general of the Shanxi Clique, chairman of Suiyuan Province from 1931, whose 35th Army was stationed at Guisui and Baotou and built irrigation works in the Hetao. In the Suiyuan Resistance of November 1936 he defeated the Puppet Mongol Army in the battles of Honggertu and Bailingmiao, winning great renown; in 1937 he fought in the battles of Xinkou and Taiyuan, and from 1938 was based in the Hetao; after the War of Resistance he became commander of the 12th War Zone. In January 1949 he led his troops to accept peaceful reorganization, and Beiping was peacefully liberated.

克什米尔.note:
Capital: Srinagar (summer), Jammu (winter)
Polity: princely state ruled by the Maharajas of the Dogra dynasty, Hindu rulers over a mostly Muslim population; the Gilgit Agency was leased to Britain in 1935 and returned in August 1947
Key figures: Maharaja Hari Singh; Sheikh Abdullah, leader of the National Conference
Key events: Pashtun tribal forces invaded in October 1947; on the 26th the Maharaja signed the instrument of accession to India, and Indian troops were airlifted to Srinagar; Gilgit went over to Pakistan in November; the ceasefire of 1 January 1949 established the ceasefire line.

克伦武装.note: The armed wing of the Karen National Union. It rose at the end of January 1949, seized Insein on the northern outskirts of Rangoon and held out against government forces for over a hundred days; it also held Toungoo and parts of the delta and Tenasserim, demanding a Karen state, “Kawthoolei”. Government forces recovered Toungoo in March 1950, and the Karen forces fell back to the Karen hills in the east and the Tenasserim mountains to carry on guerrilla warfare.

关东州.note: Kwantung Leased Territory: after the Russo-Japanese War Japan in 1905 grabbed Russia's leased territory of Lüshun and Dalian in China and set up the Kwantung Government-General; in 1919 civil and military authority were separated into the Kwantung Agency and the Kwantung Army, which is where the Kwantung Army got its name; in 1934 the Kwantung Agency was replaced by the Kwantung Bureau, under the Japanese ambassador to Puppet Manchukuo. In August 1945 Soviet troops moved into Lüshun and Dalian.

关岛.note: At the southern end of the Mariana Islands; acquired from Spain in 1898 and administered by the US Navy, it was the US outpost in the western Pacific. Japanese troops occupied it on 10 December 1941 and renamed it Omiya-jima; US forces recaptured it in August 1944, and it became one of the bases for bombing Japan.

兴安省.note: Special administrative areas set up by Puppet Manchukuo in its western regions inhabited by Mongols (today eastern Inner Mongolia): in 1932 the Xing'an Bureau and the East, South and North Xing'an branch provinces were created, and after Rehe was seized in 1933 West Xing'an Province (Kailu) was added. Mongol princes and officials served as governors, but real power lay with Japanese counsellors; the seats were scattered at Wangyemiao, Zalantun, Hailar and Kailu.

冀东政府.n: Puppet East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government
冀东政府.note:
Capital: Tongzhou (1935.11–1937.07), later moved to Tangshan (1937.08–1938.01)
Polity: the Puppet East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government, a puppet regime set up with Japanese backing when Japan engineered the North China Incident; it was established as a committee on 25 November 1935 and renamed a government on 25 December, with Yin Rugeng as chief administrator.
Territory: the twenty-two counties of the Eastern Hebei Demilitarized Zone defined by the Tanggu Truce, including Tangshan, Qinhuangdao and Shanhaiguan.
Key events: it used “East Hebei special trade” as cover for large-scale smuggling of Japanese goods, undermining China's customs revenue; on 29 July 1937 the Tongzhou peace preservation corps turned against the Japanese and rose in resistance, and Yin Rugeng was captured; in February 1938 it was merged into the Puppet Provisional Government of the Republic of China in Beiping.

冀察.note: Song Zheyuan's 29th Army system. Song Zheyuan took charge of Chahar in August 1932, was removed from office after the Zhangbei Incident of June 1935, and in August became Beiping–Tianjin Garrison Commander; on 18 December Nanjing set up the Hebei-Chahar Political Council with Song as chairman, governing Hebei, Chahar, Beiping and Tianjin with autonomy over finances and appointments, manoeuvring between Nanjing and Japan. When Beiping and Tianjin fell in July 1937, Song withdrew to Baoding and the council dissolved.

内蒙古自治政府.note: In November 1945 Ulanhu organized the Inner Mongolia Autonomy Movement Federation at Zhangjiakou, and the Chengde Conference of April 1946 merged the Eastern Mongolian Autonomous Government into it. On 1 May 1947 the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Government was established at Wangyemiao with Ulanhu as chairman, the first provincial-level ethnic autonomous government under the leadership of the Communist Party of China; in December 1949 it was renamed the People's Government of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region and moved to Zhangjiakou. In 1949–1950 the northern banners and counties of Jirim and Ju Uda Leagues and Duolun, Baochang, Huade and other places in Chahar were added in turn; in August 1952 the regional people's government moved to Guisui; in spring 1954 Suiyuan Province was abolished and its territory merged in, and in April Guisui was renamed Hohhot.

内蒙盟旗.note: The leagues and banners of Xilin Gol, Ulanqab, Ih Ju, Alxa and Ejin. Divided among the three provinces of Chahar, Suiyuan and Ningxia and ruled by jasak princes; from 1933 Prince De promoted so-called “high autonomy”.

刘存厚.note: Commander of the 2nd Division of the Sichuan Army. In July 1917 he defeated Dai Kan's Guizhou Army at Chengdu, and in December was appointed military governor of Sichuan by Beijing; in February 1918 he was driven out of Chengdu by the National Pacification Army and withdrew to Ningqiang and Hanzhong in southern Shaanxi. He returned to Sichuan as military governor in 1920 but was driven out by Sichuan Army generals in March the following year; in 1924 he became Sichuan–Shaanxi Border Defence Commissioner, holding Suiding in northern Sichuan.

加沙.note: Southern Palestine, occupied by the Egyptian army in the first Middle East war of 1948; in September the nominal All-Palestine Government was set up in Gaza; after the Israeli counter-offensives of October–December only a coastal strip remained, and with the Egyptian–Israeli armistice of February 1949 the Gaza Strip came under Egyptian military administration.

北伊朗占领区.note: From 1909 tsarist Russian troops were stationed at Tabriz, Qazvin, Rasht and elsewhere on the pretext of protecting Russian nationals; in 1911 they suppressed the Tabriz constitutionalists, and in 1912 they shelled the shrine of Imam Reza at Mashhad; in the First World War they extended to Hamadan and Kermanshah, withdrawing in early 1918. In August 1941 Soviet troops again occupied northern Iran, leaving in May 1946.

北圻.note: Its seat was Hà Nội, also the seat of the Government-General of Indochina. Nominally a protectorate, it was in fact under direct colonial rule by the French Résident supérieur. in September 1940 Japanese troops moved in; after the Japanese coup of March 1945 it passed to the Empire of Vietnam, and in August the Viet Minh led the August Revolution here and seized power. At the end of 1946 the French colonial army reoccupied Hà Nội and Hải Phòng; from 1949 it formed North Vietnam within the State of Vietnam. After the 1954 Geneva Accords the French forces regrouped in the Hà Nội–Hải Phòng area, leaving Hà Nội in October and Hải Phòng in May 1955.

北婆罗洲.note: A protectorate under the chartered rule of the British North Borneo Company, with its capital at Sandakan. Occupied by Japanese troops in January 1942; almost no one survived the Sandakan death marches on which the Japanese drove Allied prisoners of war. In July 1946 the company surrendered sovereignty and it became a Crown colony, with Labuan incorporated and the capital moved to Jesselton (now Kota Kinabalu).

北桦太.note: In July 1920 Japan, using the Nikolayevsk Incident as a pretext, invaded and occupied the northern half of Sakhalin Island and set up the military administration of the Sakhalin Expeditionary Army at Aleksandrovsk, with an eye to its oil and coal. After the Soviet–Japanese Basic Convention was signed in 1925, the Japanese troops withdrew in May in exchange for concessions on the oilfields and coalfields of northern Sakhalin.

北洋中央.note: The Beiyang Army directly controlled by Yuan Shikai and the military governors he posted to the provinces (restyled generals in 1914). After the Second Revolution its reach extended into the Yangtze River valley: Feng Guozhang in Jiangsu, Duan Zhigui and Wang Zhanyuan in Hubei, Li Chun in Jiangxi, Ni Sichong in Anhui, Tang Xiangming in Hunan, Lu Jianzhang in Shaanxi and others all belonged to it. After Yuan's death it split into the Zhili, Anhui and other warlord cliques.

北洋政府.note:
The Beijing Government of the Republic of China (Beiyang Government). Yuan Shikai took office as provisional president in Beijing in March 1912 and the Nanjing Provisional Government moved north in April; it lasted until the National Revolutionary Army entered Beijing in June 1928, and was the government of China recognized by the powers at the time.
Polity (repeatedly changed): a cabinet system under the Provisional Constitution; a presidential system under the Constitutional Compact of the Republic of China of 1914; in December 1915 Yuan Shikai restored the monarchy (Hongxian), which he was forced to abandon in March 1916.
After Yuan's death Li Yuanhong, Feng Guozhang, Xu Shichang, Cao Kun, Duan Qirui and Zhang Zuolin held power in turn; real power lay in the hands of the Beiyang warlord factions, each backed by imperialist powers.

华东解放区.note: Formed in January 1947 by merging the Shandong Liberated Area and the Jiangsu-Anhui Border Region (Central China Liberated Area), with the East China Field Army (Chen Yi, Su Yu) as its main force, which fought the Laiwu, Menglianggu, Jinan, Huaihai, Yangtze River Crossing and Shanghai campaigns. After 1949 it governed Shandong, South and North Jiangsu, South and North Anhui, Zhejiang, Fujian and Shanghai; the East China Military and Administrative Committee (Rao Shushi) was set up in January 1950, based at Shanghai. In November 1952 it became the East China Administrative Committee, and after Pingyuan Province was abolished the Heze and Liaocheng area was transferred to Shandong; it was abolished in 1954.

华中根据地.note: The New Fourth Army was formed in 1937 by reorganizing the Red Army guerrillas of eight southern provinces, with its headquarters at Yunling in southern Anhui; from 1938 it advanced behind enemy lines, opening up anti-Japanese base areas at Maoshan in southern Jiangsu, in eastern Anhui, in northern Jiangsu and elsewhere. After the KMT diehards engineered the Southern Anhui Incident in 1941, the New Fourth Army rebuilt its headquarters at Yancheng, and its base areas spread across Jiangsu, Anhui, Hubei, Henan and Zhejiang; after 1945 they became the East China and Central Plains liberated areas.

华北临时政府.note:
Seat: Beiping (renamed Beijing)
Polity: a puppet regime backed by the Japanese North China Area Army, named the “Provisional Government of the Republic of China”, with three committees (deliberative, executive and judicial) and using the Five-Coloured Flag
Key figures: Wang Kemin (chairman of the Executive Committee), Tang Erhe, Wang Yitang, Qi Xieyuan
Key events: established on 14 December 1937, governing the occupied areas of the four provinces of Hebei, Shandong, Shanxi and Henan and the two cities of Beiping and Tianjin; it absorbed the Puppet East Hebei regime in February 1938. After the Wang Jingwei Puppet Regime was set up in March 1940 it became the Puppet North China Political Council, nominally subordinate to the Wang Jingwei Puppet Regime but in fact still self-contained; it collapsed after Japan's surrender in August 1945.

华北解放区.note: Formed from the two wartime border regions of Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei and Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan. After the liberation of Shijiazhuang in November 1947 the two regions were joined into one; the North China Bureau was set up in May 1948 and the North China People's Government (Dong Biwu) in September. After the Pingjin Campaign Tianjin was liberated and Beiping peacefully liberated; the government was abolished in October 1949, and the provinces under it (Hebei, Shanxi, Pingyuan, Chahar and Suiyuan), together with Beijing and Tianjin, came directly under the Central People's Government. The North China Administrative Committee was set up in May 1952; in November the provinces of Pingyuan and Chahar were abolished, Pingyuan's Xinxiang and Anyang area going to Henan and its Heze and Liaocheng area to Shandong, and Chahar being divided between Hebei and Shanxi; in 1954 Suiyuan was merged into Inner Mongolia, and the North China Administrative Committee was abolished along with the greater administrative regions.

南伊朗占领区.note: At the end of the First World War British forces (Dunsterforce and Norperforce) were stationed along the Qazvin–Hamadan–Enzeli line, withdrawing in spring 1921. In August 1941 British troops invaded from Iraq and the Persian Gulf, occupying Khuzestan and the west and sending aid supplies to the Soviet Union through the “Persian Corridor”; they left in March 1946.

南圻.note: A French colony under direct rule with its seat at Sài Gòn, a major exporter of rice and rubber. British troops landed in September 1945 and the French colonial army promptly reoccupied it; in June 1946 France sponsored the so-called “Autonomous Republic of Cochinchina”, which was merged into the State of Vietnam in June 1949. After the 1954 Geneva Accords the Đồng Tháp Mười plain and the Cà Mau Peninsula were temporary regroupment zones for Viet Minh forces.

南洋群岛.note: South Seas Mandate: after the outbreak of the First World War the Japanese navy seized the German Marianas (except Guam), Carolines and Marshall Islands in October 1914; in 1920 they became a League of Nations Class C mandate, and in 1922 the South Seas Government was set up at Koror, Palau. After leaving the League in 1933 Japan kept hold of the islands and fortified them; in 1944 Saipan, Palau and others were captured in turn by US forces, and after the war they became a US trust territory.

南马鲁古共和国.note:
Capital: Ambon
On 25 April 1950 Ambonese former officers and men of the Dutch East Indies colonial army, together with local officials, declared “independence” from Indonesia; it was a separatist regime that sought to split Indonesia. Indonesian forces landed from July and took the town of Ambon in November; the remnants withdrew into the forests and mountains of Seram to wage guerrilla war, and their leader Soumokil was captured in December 1962.

卡塔尔.note:
Capital: Doha
Polity: sheikhdom of the Al Thani family
Key events: Ottoman troops were stationed at Doha from 1871, and Qatar was nominally part of Hasa; the Ottomans renounced it in the Anglo-Ottoman Convention of 1913, and the Ottoman garrison left in 1915; it signed a treaty with Britain in November 1916, becoming a British protectorate; the Dukhan oilfield was discovered in 1939, and oil exports began in 1949.

卡拉特.note:
Capital: Kalat
Polity: Baluch khanate, the largest princely state in the Baluchistan Agency of British India, with Makran, Kharan and Las Bela as its vassals
Key figures: the Khan, Mir Ahmad Yar Khan
Key events: declared independence on 15 August 1947; signed the instrument of accession to Pakistan on 27 March 1948, after which the Khan's brother Abdul Karim rose in revolt without success.

印度.note:
Capital: New Delhi
Polity: a dominion within the Commonwealth from 15 August 1947, with Mountbatten as first governor-general and Nehru as prime minister; a republic from 26 January 1950, when the constitution came into force, with Prasad as president
Key events: partition of India and Pakistan under the “Mountbatten Plan”, accompanied by mass migration and communal killing in the Punjab and Bengal; in 1947–1949 Patel oversaw the integration of the princely states, Junagadh and Hyderabad being incorporated by force; the Kashmir Maharaja's accession to India in October 1947 triggered the First India–Pakistan War, with a ceasefire on 1 January 1949; Gandhi assassinated in January 1948; first general election in 1951–1952, won overwhelmingly by the Congress; Andhra State created on linguistic lines in October 1953; takeover of French India in November 1954.

印度尼西亚.note:
Capital: Djakarta → Yogyakarta (1946.01–1948.12, 1949.07–12) → Djakarta
Polity: presidential republic, with Sukarno as president and Hatta as vice-president; Sjahrir and others formed cabinets in turn
Independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945, and the Indonesian people waged a war of independence, confronting the returning Dutch colonial army in Java and Sumatra; lines of demarcation were drawn twice, by the Linggadjati Agreement of 1946 and the Renville Agreement of 1948, and in July 1947 and December 1948 the Netherlands launched two colonial wars (the so-called “police actions”). After the Hague Round Table Conference the Netherlands was forced to transfer sovereignty on 27 December 1949, and the Republic of the United States of Indonesia was formed, becoming a unitary republic on 17 August 1950. Armed “Islamic State” revolts broke out in turn in West Java (August 1949), South Sulawesi and Aceh (September 1953); in December 1954 the Bogor Conference decided to convene the Asian–African Conference.

叙利亚.note:
Capital: Damascus
Polity: in October 1918 Faisal set up an Arab government in Damascus, and on 8 March 1920 he was proclaimed King of Syria; after French troops entered the city in July it became a French mandate (in reality colonial rule), divided into the states of Damascus, Aleppo, the Alawites, Jabal Druze and others; Damascus and Aleppo were merged into the State of Syria in 1925 (the Alawite State and Jabal Druze joined in 1936), and it became the Syrian Republic in 1930
Key events: the Great Syrian Revolt, a popular uprising against France, 1925–1927; captured by British and Free French forces in June–July 1941, with independence proclaimed in September; the last French troops left on 17 April 1946; joined the war against Israel in 1948; three military coups in 1949.

叙利亚起义.note: In July 1925 Sultan al-Atrash rose in Jabal Druze against French colonial rule (the mandate); after a great victory at al-Mazraa in August the revolt spread to Damascus and Hama; in October French forces bombarded Damascus, in April 1926 they retook Suwayda, and in June 1927 the revolt was put down.

台湾.note: Taiwan (under Japanese occupation): in 1895 the Qing government was forced to sign the Treaty of Shimonoseki, Taiwan was ceded and occupied, and Japan set up the Government-General of Taiwan in Taipei to impose colonial rule. Armed resistance against Japan by compatriots in Taiwan continued without let-up until it gradually subsided after the Xilai'an Uprising of 1915; the Wushe Uprising broke out in 1930. After 1937 Japan forced through imperialization and used Taiwan as a base for its southward advance. On 25 October 1945 the Chinese government accepted the Japanese surrender in Taipei; Taiwan was restored and returned to Chinese territory.

台湾省.note: Taiwan was restored to China on 25 October 1945; the Nationalist Government set up the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Executive Office (Chen Yi), replaced in 1947 by the Taiwan Provincial Government. At the end of 1949 the KMT authorities retreated to Taiwan.

吉兰.note:
Capital: Rasht
Polity: Persian Socialist Soviet Republic
Key figures: Mirza Kuchik Khan (Jangali movement), Iranian communists
Key events: from 1915 the Jangalis resisted British and Russian imperialism from the forests of Gilan; in May 1920 the Soviet Russian Caspian Flotilla landed at Enzeli, and the republic was proclaimed in June; after Soviet Russia concluded a treaty with Persia in February 1921 it withdrew its troops, and the republic was torn by internal strife; that autumn Reza Khan put it down with the Cossack Division, and Kuchik Khan froze to death in the mountains.

吉尔伯特.note: A British colony, with its seat on Ocean Island (Banaba). Japanese troops took Makin in December 1941 and Tarawa and Ocean Island in 1942; US forces captured Tarawa and Makin in November 1943, but the Japanese on Ocean Island did not surrender until October 1945.

吉尔吉斯.note: The Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast (renamed the Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast the following year) was set up in October 1924 within the Russian Federation; in February 1926 it became an autonomous republic, and its capital Pishpek was renamed Frunze; in December 1936 it was raised to a union republic.

吉林孟恩远.note: The Beiyang veteran Meng Enyuan was military governor of Jilin in 1915–1919, contending with Zhang Zuolin for the Northeast. In July 1919 Zhang Zuolin used a transfer order from Beijing to force him out; his subordinate Gao Shibin resisted and failed, and Jilin passed to the Fengtian Clique.

呼伦贝尔自治.note: Jurisdiction of the Hulunbuir Deputy Lieutenant-General, the pastures of the Barga, Solun and Ölöd tribes, with its seat at Hailar. In January 1912, instigated by tsarist Russia, it drove out the Qing officials and declared “independence”, attaching itself to Outer Mongolia; in November 1915 China and Russia concluded the Hulunbuir Agreement, making it a special region, nominally under the central government but in fact controlled by tsarist Russia. Abolished in 1920.

哈塔伊.note: Created in September 1938 from the Alexandretta district of French Syria, with its capital at Antioch; France and Turkey jointly garrisoned it, and its assembly was dominated by Turks. On 29 June 1939 the assembly voted to join Turkey; France acquiesced in order to keep Turkey on the side of Britain and France in the European war, but Syria did not recognize the annexation.

唐努乌梁海.note:
The Tuvan lands on the upper Yenisei River, under the jurisdiction of the Uliassutai General in the Qing period. After the fall of the Qing some chiefs attached themselves to Outer Mongolia and others sought Russian protection; in April 1914 tsarist Russia forcibly placed the region under its “protection”, set up the Uriankhai Krai and built Belotsarsk (present-day Kyzyl).
During the Russian Civil War the Beijing Government sent troops to garrison it for a time; in 1921 the so-called “Tannu Tuva People's Republic” was set up with the backing of Soviet Russia, and in 1944 it was annexed by the Soviet Union.

唐生智.note: Tang Shengzhi's forces in Hunan. In 1926 he drove out Zhao Hengti and took charge of Hunan, soon joining the Nationalist Government as the Eighth Army; in the Northern Expedition it was first into Changsha and Hankou, and his power extended over Hunan and Hubei. During the split between Nanjing and Wuhan it was Wuhan's main military force; it defied orders in October 1927 and was defeated by the Western Expedition Army in November, and Tang fled. In 1929 he returned to command his old troops in eastern Hebei, and in December rose against Chiang at Zhengzhou and failed.

四川自治.note:
After the Sichuan Army drove out the Yunnan and Guizhou armies at the end of 1920, Sichuan's generals advocated “Sichuan ruled by Sichuanese”; from 1921 they obeyed the orders of neither Beijing nor Guangzhou, and a commander-in-chief of the Sichuan Army who was also civil governor held the armies together.
Key figures: Liu Xiang (commander-in-chief and civil governor from June 1921), Liu Chengxun, Xiong Kewu, Yang Sen.
In reality it was a “garrison-area system” under which the warlord factions carved up the province; it gradually split after the War of the First and Second Armies in 1922. In 1923 Xiong Kewu was appointed by Sun Yat-sen to campaign against the rebels while Yang Sen, Liu Xiang and others leaned on the Zhili Clique, and self-government existed in name only.

四川讨袁军.note: On 4 August 1913 Xiong Kewu, with the 5th Division of the Sichuan Army, declared independence at Chongqing to campaign against Yuan; he attacked westward against Luzhou and Neijiang without taking them, abandoned the city on 11 September and fled, and Yunnan and Guizhou troops entered Chongqing.

国民军.note: After launching the Beijing Coup in October 1924, Feng Yuxiang combined his troops with those of Hu Jingyi and Sun Yue as the Guominjun of the Republic of China, with Feng as commander-in-chief and commander of the First Army, and Hu and Sun commanding the Second and Third Armies. The First Army held the capital region, Chahar and Suiyuan, taking Gansu in 1925; the Second Army held Henan, and the Third Army entered Shaanxi. After taking Tianjin at the end of 1925 it came under the combined attack of the Fengtian, Zhili, Zhili-Shandong and Shanxi armies; in spring 1926 the Second Army disintegrated in Henan, and in April the First Army withdrew from Beijing to hold Nankou, retreating west in August. In September Feng Yuxiang, back from the Soviet Union, took the oath at Wuyuan and renamed his force the Guominjun Allied Army, joining the National Revolution; it was later called the Second Army Group and the Northwestern Army, and disintegrated after its defeat in the Central Plains War of 1930.

国民政府.note:
The regime established by the Kuomintang of China, passing through the Constitution Protection Military Government, the Generalissimo's Headquarters, the Guangzhou Nationalist Government, the Wuhan Nationalist Government and the Nanjing Nationalist Government.
Capital: Guangzhou (1917–1926) → Wuhan (1927) → Nanjing (1927–1937) → Chongqing (1937–1946) → Nanjing (1946–1949); in December 1949 the KMT authorities retreated to Taiwan.
Polity: in 1917 Sun Yat-sen organized the Constitution Protection Military Government in Guangzhou; in 1923 the Generalissimo's Headquarters was set up, reorganized in July 1925 as the Nationalist Government, ruling the state through the party; from 1928 came political tutelage and the five-yuan system, with one-party dictatorship by the KMT; the constitution came into force in 1947.
Key figures: Sun Yat-sen, Wang Jingwei, Hu Hanmin, Chiang Kai-shek, Lin Sen, Li Zongren.
Key events: the first KMT–CPC cooperation in 1924 and the Northern Expedition in 1926; in 1927 Chiang Kai-shek launched the April 12 Counter-revolutionary Coup and the Wang Jingwei clique carried out the July 15 “purge of Communists”; the Nanjing and Wuhan governments merged, and the Great Revolution failed. The Northeast Flag Replacement of 1928 nominally unified the country; thereafter the new warlords fought one another year after year, and KMT forces launched five “encirclement” campaigns against the revolutionary base areas. In 1937–1945, during the second KMT–CPC cooperation, KMT forces bore the fighting on the frontal battlefield, and in 1943 new treaties were concluded with Britain and the United States; in 1946 it launched a full-scale civil war, was defeated in the War of Liberation, and in December 1949 retreated to Taiwan.

土属亚美尼亚俄占区.note: The eastern Ottoman provinces captured by the tsarist Russian Caucasus Army in the First World War: Bayazid in 1914, Van in 1915, and Erzurum, Trebizond and Erzincan in 1916, organized as the military Governor-Generalship of “Turkish Armenia”. The Russian army disintegrated in 1917, and the Ottoman army recovered the area in February–April 1918.

土库曼.note: Established in the national delimitation of October 1924, with its capital at Poltoratsk (renamed Ashkhabad again in 1927); it comprised the former Transcaspian Oblast and the Turkmen-inhabited areas of Bukhara and Khorezm.

土耳其.note:
Capital: Ankara (seat of the Grand National Assembly from 1920, declared the capital on 13 October 1923)
Polity: Grand National Assembly government from 23 April 1920; republic proclaimed on 29 October 1923 with Mustafa Kemal as president; one-party rule by the Republican People's Party until 1946
Key events: in 1919–1922 Kemal led the national liberation war (the War of Independence), beating back Armenia, France and Greece in turn; the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923 fixed the borders and abolished consular jurisdiction; the caliphate was abolished in 1924 and secularizing reforms were carried out; Kemal died in 1938 and was succeeded by İnönü; Hatay was annexed in 1939; long neutral in the Second World War, it declared war on Germany in February 1945.

埃及.note: This map covers only the Sinai Peninsula and the east bank of the Suez Canal; the capital, Cairo, is off the map. Occupied by British troops from 1882, Egypt was nominally a khedivate under Ottoman suzerainty; Britain declared it a protectorate in December 1914; on 28 February 1922 Britain unilaterally declared Egypt independent and Fuad took the title of king, while Britain retained its rights over the canal, defence and other matters; after the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 British troops were confined to the Canal Zone. Egypt sent troops into Palestine in 1948 and after the war controlled the Gaza Strip.

塔吉克.note: The Tajik Autonomous Republic was set up in October 1924 within Uzbekistan, with its capital at Dushanbe (renamed Stalinabad in 1929); in October 1929 the Khujand area was added and it was raised to a union republic. The Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Oblast was set up in the Pamirs.

塘沽停战区.note: The demilitarized zone drawn by the Tanggu Truce of 31 May 1933 south of the Great Wall and east of the Yanqing–Tongzhou–Lutai line: the twenty-two counties of eastern Hebei. Chinese forces withdrew, leaving only peace preservation corps to keep order, while Japanese forces could “inspect” the zone at any time, gravely impairing China's sovereignty. In November 1935 Yin Rugeng set up the Puppet East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government here.

塞浦路斯.note: Under the Cyprus Convention of 1878 the Ottomans handed it over to British administration, nominal sovereignty remaining with the sultan; Britain declared its annexation on 5 November 1914, and it became a Crown colony in 1925. In 1931 the Greek Cypriots' demand for union with Greece (“enosis”) led to the October riots.

外蒙北洋.note: In November 1919, under pressure from Xu Shuzheng, the princes of Outer Mongolia petitioned to cancel “autonomy”; the Beijing Government restored its jurisdiction, placing the region under the Northwest Frontier Commissioner, garrisoning Urga and controlling Uriankhai. After the Zhili–Anhui War of 1920 Xu Shuzheng left office and an Urga–Uliassutai–Kobdo–Tannu Pacification Commissioner was appointed instead; in February 1921 Ungern's White Russian forces took Urga, and the Beijing Government's jurisdiction over Outer Mongolia was cut off.

外蒙古.note:
Centre: Urga (renamed Ulan Bator in 1924). Formerly the four Khalkha aimags of the Qing and the territory under Kobdo.
In December 1911, instigated by tsarist Russia, the princes of Outer Mongolia declared “independence” and enthroned the Jebtsundamba Khutughtu as Bogd Khan; they took Kobdo in 1912 and invaded Inner Mongolia without success in 1913. After the Kyakhta Agreement between China, Russia and Mongolia was signed in 1915, “independence” was cancelled and “autonomy” was practised under the suzerainty of the Republic of China; in 1919 the autonomy was cancelled under pressure.
In 1921 the Soviet Russian Red Army and the armed forces of the Mongolian People's Party entered Urga, and Outer Mongolia again declared “independence”; in 1924 the Mongolian People's Republic was established. A plebiscite was held in October 1945, and in January 1946 the Nationalist Government recognized its independence.

外里海.note:
Capital: Ashkhabad
Polity: Socialist Revolutionary–Menshevik counter-revolutionary government set up after the overthrow of the local soviet in July 1918
Key events: backed by the British interventionist Malleson Mission and British Indian troops; in September it killed the captured Baku commissars (the 26 Baku Commissars); British troops withdrew in 1919, and the Red Army took Ashkhabad in July; the remnants, with Denikin's forces, held Krasnovodsk until its fall in February 1920.

大汉四川军政府.note: On 27 November 1911 the Viceroy of Sichuan, Zhao Erfeng, was forced to hand over power, and the constitutionalist Pu Dianjun became military governor; after the Chengdu mutiny of 8 December Yin Changheng succeeded him, and on the 22nd had Zhao Erfeng executed. Merged with Chongqing in 1912, and in March renamed the Sichuan Military Governorate of the Republic of China.

大韩民国.note:
Capital: Seoul (during the Korean War the government moved south to Daejeon, Daegu and Busan; Busan was the provisional capital from January 1951 to August 1953)
Polity: presidential republic; first president Syngman Rhee
In May 1948 a separate election was held south of the 38th parallel under the supervision of the US-manipulated UN Temporary Commission on Korea; the state was founded on 15 August, and in December the UN General Assembly recognized it as the lawful government of the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. In June 1950 the Korean civil war broke out and the United States intervened militarily; the ROK Army at one point fell back to the Busan Perimeter; after the US Incheon landing in September it retook Seoul and advanced north with the US-led “UN Command” forces. Seoul was lost again in January 1951 and retaken in March. In the Busan political crisis of 1952 Syngman Rhee used martial law to force through a constitutional amendment introducing direct presidential elections. At the armistice of July 1953 Syngman Rhee refused to sign the Armistice Agreement, and in October he concluded the Mutual Defense Treaty with the United States; the so-called “recovered areas” north of the 38th parallel were handed over by the “UN Command” to ROK administration in November 1954.

奉系.note: The northeastern warlord group headed by Zhang Zuolin, backed by Japan. Zhang Zuolin, who began as a bandit, became military governor of Fengtian in 1916, took Heilongjiang and Jilin in 1917–1919 to unify the Three Northeastern Provinces, and became Inspector-General of the Three Northeastern Provinces in 1918. In 1920 he helped the Zhili Clique defeat the Anhui Clique and shared control of the Beijing Government with it; defeated in the First Zhili–Fengtian War of 1922, he withdrew beyond the Great Wall, declared the “autonomy” of the Three Northeastern Provinces and rebuilt his army. Victorious in the Second Zhili–Fengtian War of 1924, he entered North China, his power reaching for a time as far south as Jiangsu and Shanghai. In 1925 he was driven out of Jiangnan by Sun Chuanfang and was nearly destroyed by Guo Songling's revolt against Fengtian; in 1926, allied with the Zhili Clique, he attacked the Guominjun and re-entered Beijing, and in 1927 formed the Anguojun Military Government. In June 1928 Zhang Zuolin was killed in a bombing by the Japanese Kwantung Army at Huanggutun; Zhang Xueliang succeeded him, and with the Northeast Flag Replacement in December the army was renamed the Northeastern Army.

奥斯曼.note:
Capital: Constantinople (Istanbul)
Polity: constitutional monarchy under the sultan-caliph; the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 restored the constitution, and after the Raid on the Sublime Porte in January 1913 Enver, Talat and Djemal, the “Three Pashas”, ruled as dictators
Key events: lost Libya and the Dodecanese in the Italo-Turkish War of 1911–1912 and most of its European territory in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913; entered the war on the side of the Central Powers in November 1914, and from 1915 deported and massacred the Armenians; with the Armistice of Mudros in October 1918 it lost all its Arab provinces, and the capital was occupied by the Allies; signed the Treaty of Sèvres in August 1920; the sultanate was abolished on 1 November 1922.

奥里萨.note: Separated from the Bihar and Orissa Province on 1 April 1936 and enlarged with Ganjam and other areas of the Madras Presidency, it was formed as a province on the basis of the Oriya language, with its capital at Cuttack.

威克岛.note: A central Pacific atoll, taken by the United States in 1899; Pan American Airways set up a flying-boat staging station there in 1935, and US Marines were stationed there in 1941. It fell to the second Japanese landing on 23 December; the Japanese renamed it Otori-shima and held out there, cut off, until September 1945.

威海卫.note: Forcibly leased by Britain in 1898, facing Lüshun across the Bohai Strait; it was the summer anchorage of Britain's Far East fleet and was governed by a commissioner sent by the Colonial Office. Returned to China on 1 October 1930 and made the Weihaiwei Administrative Region, though some facilities on Liugong Island were lent to the Royal Navy for a further ten years. Occupied by Japanese troops in March 1938.

孙传芳.note: The Zhili Clique warlord Sun Chuanfang entered Zhejiang from Fujian in 1924, drove out the Fengtian Army in 1925 and made himself commander-in-chief of the Five-Province Allied Army of Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Jiangxi and Fujian, based at Nanjing. In the Northern Expedition he lost his main force in the Jiangxi campaign; in 1927 he fell back to hold the north bank of the Yangtze, was crushingly defeated after crossing the river at Longtan in August, and his remaining troops went over to Zhang Zongchang; after the Northern Expedition was completed in 1928 he left for Dalian.

孟买.note: Capital at Bombay; it covered Gujarat, Maharashtra and northern Karnataka, and Sind until 1936. India's centre of textiles and finance; the Congress was founded here in 1885, and the “Quit India” resolution was also passed here in August 1942.

孟加拉.note: The Bengal Presidency, where Calcutta, the capital of British India until 1911, lay. In 1905 Curzon pursued “divide and rule”, splitting off a separate province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, which provoked the anti-partition movement; Bengal was reunited in April 1912, while Bihar and Orissa were separated from it. It suffered the great famine of 1943, and at the 1947 partition West Bengal went to India.

宁海.note: In the early Republic the Qinghai Administrator governed the Mongol and Tibetan tribes of Qinghai, but real power lay with Ma Qi, brigade general of the Xining garrison; in 1915 Ma Qi became Garrison Commissioner of Ninghai on the Gansu frontier, and from then on the Ma warlords of Hehuang ruled Qinghai.

宁马.note: The Ningxia Ma family army. Ma Fuxiang was Defence Commissioner of Ningxia in the early Republic, and his son Ma Hongkui and nephew Ma Hongbin commanded the troops in turn, at one time attaching themselves to the Guominjun and the Northwestern Army. Ningxia became a province in 1929; after the Northwestern Army disintegrated in 1930 Ma Hongbin governed Ningxia, and in 1933 Ma Hongkui succeeded him as provincial chairman, ruling Ningxia until 1949.

安达曼.note: Capital at Port Blair, where Britain built the Cellular Jail to hold political prisoners of the Indian national movement. Occupied by Japanese troops in March 1942 and nominally handed over in December 1943 to Bose's Provisional Government of Free India; British forces recovered the islands in October 1945.

察南自治政府.note: A puppet regime set up at Zhangjiakou with the backing of the Kwantung Army on 4 September 1937, with Yu Pinqing as supreme commissioner, governing ten counties south of the Great Wall including Xuanhua, Huailai and Yuxian. It joined the Puppet Mengjiang United Committee in November and was merged into the Puppet Mengjiang United Autonomous Government in September 1939.

察哈尔抗日同盟军.n: Chahar People's Anti-Japanese Allied Army (Feng Yuxiang)
察哈尔抗日同盟军.note: Formed at Zhangjiakou on 26 May 1933 by Feng Yuxiang in cooperation with the Communist Party of China, with Ji Hongchang and Fang Zhenwu as front-line commanders. In July it recovered Kangbao, Baochang, Guyuan and Duolun, but soon came under attack from both Japanese forces and KMT forces; in August Feng Yuxiang stepped down, and the Allied Army was defeated.

小巽他.note: Bali, Lombok, Sumbawa, Flores, Sumba and West Timor, with seats mostly at Singaraja and Kupang. Japanese troops landed on Bali and Timor in February 1942; Dutch forces returned to Bali in March 1946.

小笠原美军.note: In February–March 1945 US forces captured Iwo Jima, using it as an emergency landing field for B-29s bombing the Japanese home islands and as a base for escort fighters; the Japanese garrison on Chichijima surrendered in September. In January 1946 a GHQ directive separated the islands from Japanese administration and placed them under the US Navy. They remained under US administration after the San Francisco Peace Treaty; apart from a few descendants of Western settlers, the islanders were not allowed to return. The islands were returned to Japan in 1968.

尼泊尔.note:
Capital: Kathmandu
Polity: the Shah dynasty kings were figureheads, while the Rana family monopolized power as hereditary prime ministers (1846–1951)
Key events: allied with British India, supplying Gurkha soldiers to the British army and sending troops to aid Britain in both world wars; the Anglo-Nepalese Treaty of December 1923 confirmed Nepal's independence; in November 1950 King Tribhuvan took refuge in the Indian embassy and then left the country, the Nepali Congress rose in revolt, and the Rana dictatorship ended in February the following year.

山东根据地.note: At the end of 1937 and the beginning of 1938 the CPC Shandong Provincial Committee launched anti-Japanese armed uprisings at Mount Tianfu, Mount Heitie, Mount Culai and elsewhere, forming the Shandong Column of the Eighth Route Army; in 1939 the main force of the 115th Division entered Shandong. The base area was centred on the Yimeng Mountains, with further areas such as Jiaodong and Qinghe. In 1940 the Shandong Provincial Wartime Work Promotion Committee was set up; after 1945 it formed the main body of the East China Liberated Area.

川军刘文辉.note: Liu Wenhui, a native of Dayi, Sichuan, was Liu Xiang's clan uncle. Rising from brigade commander in the early 1920s, he held Xufu (Yibin) as his garrison area; he joined in overthrowing Yang Sen in 1925 and in driving out the Guizhou Army in 1926, expanding into western and southern Sichuan, and at the end of the year became commander of the 24th Army of the National Revolutionary Army. In 1929 he became chairman of the Sichuan provincial government, also holding the Sichuan Frontier. Defeated by Liu Xiang in the War of the Two Lius in 1932–1933, he fell back to Xikang, and in 1939 became chairman of the Xikang provincial government. In December 1949 he, Deng Xihou and Pan Wenhua announced their uprising by circular telegram at Pengxian, and Xikang was thereupon peacefully liberated.

川军刘湘.note: Liu Xiang, a native of Dayi, Sichuan, was leader of the Second Army of the Sichuan Army. In 1920 he allied with Xiong Kewu to drive out the Yunnan and Guizhou armies, and in 1921 became commander-in-chief of the Sichuan Army and civil governor, presiding over Sichuan self-government; he stepped down for a time during the War of the First and Second Armies in 1922, and in 1923, attaching himself to Wu Peifu, became Rehabilitation Commissioner of Sichuan and joined Yang Sen in driving out Xiong Kewu. In 1925 he allied with Yuan Zuming's Guizhou Army to overthrow Yang Sen, and in 1926 drove out the Guizhou Army; with Chongqing as his base, he changed flags at the end of the year and became commander of the 21st Army of the National Revolutionary Army. He defeated Liu Wenhui in the War of the Two Lius in 1932–1933, became chairman of the Sichuan provincial government in 1935 and unified Sichuan's administration; after the outbreak of the nationwide War of Resistance he led the Sichuan Army out of Sichuan to fight Japan, and died of illness at Hankou in January 1938.

川军诸部.note: The Sichuan Army forces other than those of Liu Xiang and Liu Wenhui under Sichuan's garrison-area system, chiefly Xiong Kewu, Liu Chengxun, Deng Xihou (28th Army), Tian Songyao (29th Army), Liu Cunhou (23rd Army, Suiding in northern Sichuan), Yang Sen (20th Army), Lai Xinhui and others. After Xiong Kewu took charge of Sichuan in 1918, each army marked out a garrison area where it stood and levied taxes there, and the warlords fought dozens of wars. Deng, Tian and Liu Wenhui jointly held Chengdu from 1926; after the War of the Two Lius in 1932–1933 they submitted to Liu Xiang. In 1935 the KMT Central Army entered Sichuan and Sichuan's administration was unified; the armies were reorganized, and after the outbreak of the nationwide War of Resistance they went to the front.

川督.note: The Sichuan Military Governorate of the early Republic. In 1912 Yin Changheng and Hu Jingyi were military governors in turn, Hu Jingyi attaching himself to Yuan Shikai; in 1915 Yuan Shikai sent Chen Yi with three Beiyang brigades into Sichuan to take charge. During the National Protection War Chen Yi declared Sichuan independent on 22 May 1916.

川西北红军.note: In spring 1935 the Red Fourth Front Army left the Sichuan-Shaanxi Soviet Area, crossed the Jialing River westward and held the Maoxian, Lixian and Maogong area; in June it joined forces with the Central Red Army. After Zhang Guotao refused to go north and led the army south to defeat, in spring 1936 it moved to Dawu, Luhuo and Garze, and in July joined the Red Second and Sixth Army Groups and marched north.

川边.note: Jurisdiction of the Sichuan–Yunnan Frontier Commissioner (present-day Garze, Sichuan, and Qamdo, Xizang). After the Batang Incident of 1905 Zhao Erfeng replaced the native chieftains here with regular officials, and in 1909–1911 pushed on to Chamdo (Qamdo), Dege and Zhag'yab. Under the Republic it became the Sichuan Frontier Pacification Office; in 1914 the Sichuan Frontier Special Region was set up, directly under the Beijing Government.

川陕苏区.note: The Sichuan-Shaanxi Revolutionary Base Area, built by the Red Fourth Front Army (Xu Xiangqian, Chen Changhao, Zhang Guotao) after it entered northern Sichuan in December 1932; the Sichuan-Shaanxi Provincial Soviet was set up at Tongjiang in February 1933. Centred on Tongjiang, Nanjiang and Bazhong, it expanded after a string of victories in autumn 1933 to Xuanhan, Daxian and Yingshan, its population at one point approaching five million. It defeated Tian Songyao's three-pronged offensive and Liu Xiang's six-pronged offensive in turn, and was abandoned after the Red Fourth Front Army crossed the Jialing River westward in April 1935.

左右江苏区.note: The Baise Uprising of December 1929 created the Red Seventh Army and the Youjiang Soviet, and the Longzhou Uprising of February 1930 created the Red Eighth Army and the Zuojiang Revolutionary Committee; together they were called the Zuojiang-Youjiang Base Area, with Donglan and Fengshan at the core of the Youjiang area. In October 1930 the Red Seventh Army was ordered north, and Wei Baqun stayed behind in the Youjiang area with the 21st Division; he gave his life in 1932.

巴勒斯坦.note: Occupied by British forces in 1917–1918, with a civil administration from July 1920; the League of Nations mandate of 1922 incorporated the Balfour Declaration. Jewish immigration grew steadily; there were Arab riots in 1929 and the great Arab revolt of 1936–1939; the White Paper of 1939 restricted immigration, and in 1944–1947 Jewish armed groups fought the British. The UN General Assembly adopted the partition resolution in November 1947, and the mandate ended on 14 May 1948.

巴基斯坦.note:
Capital: Karachi
Polity: dominion within the Commonwealth, established on 14 August 1947
Key figures: Jinnah (governor-general, died September 1948), Liaquat Ali Khan (prime minister)
Key events: made up of Sind, Baluchistan, the North-West Frontier Province and West Punjab in the west and East Bengal in the east, the two wings some 1,600 km apart; in 1947–1948 it contested Kashmir with India, gaining control of its western and northern parts; Kalat and the other Baluch princely states acceded in March 1948; after Liaquat's assassination in October 1951 the governor-general, the bureaucracy and the military gradually took real power; the Bengali Language Movement erupted in Dacca in February 1952, and the Muslim League was crushed in the East Bengal elections of 1954; in the same year Pakistan joined the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization.

巴布亚.note: Southeastern New Guinea; a British protectorate from 1884, transferred to Australia in 1906, with its seat at Port Moresby. In 1942 Japanese troops crossed the Owen Stanley Range to attack Port Moresby but were checked on the Kokoda Track and at Milne Bay.

巴控克什米尔.note: In October 1947 tribal forces and Poonch insurgents entered Kashmir, and on the 24th an “Azad Kashmir” government was proclaimed; in November the Gilgit Scouts went over to Pakistan, and in August 1948 they took Skardu. After the ceasefire of January 1949 the area came under Pakistani administration.

巴斯马奇.note: A collective term for the anti-Soviet Muslim armed groups of Central Asia (Turkic for “raiders”). They arose in Fergana after the Kokand Autonomy was crushed in 1918, under leaders such as Madamin Bek and Kurshirmat; after 1920 their centre of gravity shifted to Eastern Bukhara; Enver Pasha joined them at the end of 1921 and for a time took Dushanbe, but was killed in action in August 1922; Ibrahim Bek held out until 1931.

巴林.note: A sheikhdom of the Al Khalifa family, a British protectorate after the exclusive agreements of 1880 and 1892; in 1946 the British Political Resident in the Persian Gulf moved from Bushire to Bahrain. Oil was discovered in 1932, the earliest on the Arabian side of the Persian Gulf.

巴特寮.note:
Capital: the mountains around Sam Neua (from 1953)
Polity: the Lao Resistance Government and the Lao Freedom Front (founded August 1950), led by Prince Souphanouvong; allied with the Democratic Republic of Vietnam and fighting France side by side with the Vietnam People's Army
In April 1953 it advanced into Upper Laos with the Vietnam People's Army, making Sam Neua its base; from late 1953 to early 1954 the Vietnam People's Army again entered Central and Upper Laos, at one point reaching Thakhek and the outskirts of Luang Prabang. The Geneva Accords of July 1954 had its forces regroup in the two provinces of Sam Neua and Phongsaly, nominally still part of the Kingdom of Laos, pending a political settlement.

布哈拉.note:
Capital: Bukhara
Polity: emirate of the Manghit dynasty, reduced to a protectorate of tsarist Russia in 1868; became the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic in October 1920
Key figures: the last emir, Alim Khan; the Young Bukharan Fayzulla Khodzhayev
Key events: at the end of August 1920 the Young Bukharans rose up, and on 2 September Frunze took Bukhara with the Red Army; the emir fled east to Dushanbe and in March of the following year escaped to Afghanistan; the Basmachi resistance in Eastern Bukhara went on until the mid-1920s; abolished after the national delimitation of 1924.

希瓦.note:
Capital: Khiva
Polity: khanate of the Qungrat dynasty, reduced to a protectorate of tsarist Russia in 1873; became the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic in April 1920
Key events: from 1918 the Turkmen leader Junaid Khan held the khan's court in his grip and wielded real power; in February 1920 the Red Army and the Young Khivans broke into Khiva and the khan abdicated; in the national delimitation of 1924 its territory was divided among the Uzbek and Turkmen republics and the Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast.

希腊.note: This map covers only the eastern Aegean islands and Asia Minor. In the First Balkan War of 1912 Greece took Lesbos, Chios, Samos and other islands; in May 1919, with Allied support, it invaded Smyrna, and the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920 gave it Eastern Thrace and the administration of Smyrna; it drove deep into Anatolia in 1920–1921 but was defeated by the Turkish army in August–September 1922; in 1923 it exchanged populations with Turkey. Occupied by Germany and Italy in 1941 and liberated in October 1944; it took over the Dodecanese in March 1947 and formally annexed them in 1948.

广州国民政府.note:
The regime of Guangdong and Guangxi during the Nanjing–Guangzhou confrontation of 1931.
After Hu Hanmin was placed under house arrest at Tangshan in February, Wang Jingwei, Sun Fo, Tang Shaoyi, Chen Jitang, Li Zongren and others convened an Extraordinary Conference of the Central Executive and Supervisory Committees in Guangzhou on 27 May, and the next day set up a Nationalist Government in opposition to Nanjing. It governed Guangdong and Guangxi, and commissioned Shi Yousan and other northern generals to oppose Chiang.
After the September 18 Incident the two sides held peace talks in Shanghai; Chiang Kai-shek stepped down in December, and the Guangzhou Nationalist Government was dissolved on 1 January 1932 and replaced by the Southwest Executive Headquarters and the Southwest Political Council. Guangdong and Guangxi remained semi-independent until 1936.

广州湾.note: In November 1899 France forced the Qing government to sign the Guangzhouwan Lease Convention, leasing the territory for 99 years; it was attached to French Indochina, with its capital at Fort-Bayard (now Xiashan, Zhanjiang). Early in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression it served as South China's outlet to the outside world and as a smuggling port; in February 1943 Japanese troops moved in, and in August 1945 China and France signed an agreement returning it, after which Zhanjiang City was set up.

建国粤军.n: Guangdong Army for National Construction (Xu Chongzhi)
建国粤军.note: Xu Chongzhi's Guangdong Army. In 1922 he led the Northern Expedition Army into southern Jiangxi; after Chen Jiongming's rebellion he turned back but failed, moved into Fujian and in October took Fuzhou with Wang Yongquan, styling his force the Eastern Route Anti-Rebel Army. Returning to Guangdong in 1923 as the Guangdong Army for National Construction, it fought Chen Jiongming along the Dong River. In September 1925 Xu Chongzhi was forced to leave Guangdong, and his troops were incorporated into the National Revolutionary Army.

德国.note: German Empire → Weimar Republic (1918.11) → Nazi Germany (1933). In China it held Jiaozhou Bay and concessions in Tianjin and Hankou; Qingdao fell in November 1914, China declared war on Germany in 1917 and recovered the concessions, and under the Sino-German Agreement of 1921 Germany gave up extraterritoriality. In the 1930s a German advisory mission helped the Nationalist Government reorganize its army; in 1938 the mission was recalled and Germany recognized Puppet Manchukuo.

德属新几内亚.note: Germany's Pacific colony: northeastern New Guinea (Kaiser-Wilhelmsland), the Bismarck Archipelago and Bougainville; it held the Marshall Islands from 1885 and in 1899 bought the Carolines, Palau and the Marianas (except Guam) from Spain; seat at Rabaul. After the outbreak of the First World War, in September–October 1914 the part south of the equator was occupied by Australian forces and the part north of it by the Japanese navy.

德鲁兹山.note: In 1921 France set up the Jabal Druze State centred on Suwayda; in 1925 Sultan al-Atrash launched the Great Syrian Revolt here; it was merged into Syria in 1936 (separated again for a time in 1939–1942).

意大利.note: This map covers only the Aegean and Asia Minor. In 1911–1912 Italy launched the Italo-Turkish War, seizing Tripolitania and Cyrenaica (off the map) and the Dodecanese, with Rhodes as the capital; in 1919–1921, on the basis of secret Allied agreements, it occupied the Antalya region before withdrawing; the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 confirmed the Dodecanese as Italian. It occupied Samos in 1941; after Italy's surrender in September 1943 the Aegean islands were seized by German troops.

所罗门.note: A British protectorate from 1893, with its seat at Tulagi. Japanese troops took Tulagi in May 1942; in August US forces landed on Guadalcanal, and after six months of bitter fighting the Japanese withdrew; after the war the seat moved to Honiara.

扩大会议.note:
The regime of the anti-Chiang factions during the Central Plains War of 1930.
Amid the wars among the new warlords, on 13 July Wang Jingwei's Reorganizationists and the Western Hills Group, together with Yan Xishan and Feng Yuxiang, convened the Enlarged Conference of the Central Party Headquarters of the Kuomintang of China in Beiping; on 9 September they organized a Nationalist Government with Yan Xishan as chairman and Wang Jingwei, Feng Yuxiang, Li Zongren and others as members.
