It governed Shanxi, Hebei, Chahar and Suiyuan, Beiping and Tianjin, northern Shandong, most of Henan and the northwestern provinces. On 18 September Zhang Xueliang declared his support for Chiang by circular telegram and the Northeastern Army entered North China; the Enlarged Conference moved to Taiyuan and dissolved in late October, and in November Yan and Feng announced their retirement by circular telegram.

护国军.note:
The army formed to oppose Yuan Shikai's restoration of the monarchy after Tang Jiyao, Cai E and Li Liejun declared Yunnan independent at Kunming on 25 December 1915. It was divided into three armies: Cai E's First Army entered Sichuan, Li Liejun's Second Army advanced into Guangdong and Guangxi, and Tang Jiyao's Third Army stayed behind to hold Yunnan.
Guizhou, Guangxi, Guangdong, Zhejiang, Shaanxi, Sichuan and Hunan declared independence one after another, and on 8 May 1916 the Military Affairs Council was set up at Zhaoqing, with Tang Jiyao as chief commander and Cen Chunxuan as deputy chief commander.
Yuan Shikai died of illness in June and Li Yuanhong succeeded him; in July the Military Affairs Council was dissolved and the provinces revoked their independence.

护国第一军.note: In January 1916 Cai E led three brigade groups of the Yunnan Army into Sichuan, attacking Xuzhou and Luzhou and fighting the Beiyang Army to a stalemate at Naxi; after the ceasefire in late March it held the Xuyong area of southern Sichuan, and entered Luzhou after Yuan Shikai's death.

拉希德.note:
Capital: Ha'il
Polity: emirate of the Rashidi family of the Shammar tribe, pro-Ottoman
Key events: for a time in the late 19th century it swallowed up the Saudi state, but after 1902 it was gradually overpowered by Ibn Saud, losing Qassim in 1906; sided with the Ottomans in the First World War; amid incessant feuds within the ruling family, Ha'il surrendered to Ibn Saud on 2 November 1921 and the emirate came to an end.

拉杰普塔纳.note: More than twenty Rajput princely states, including Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bikaner and Jaisalmer, with the British Agent to the Governor-General at Mount Abu. They joined India in 1947 and were combined into the state of Rajasthan in 1949.

掸邦.note: States of Shan hereditary chiefs (saopha) under indirect British rule; in 1922 they formed the Federated Shan States, with its seat at Taunggyi. Thai troops took Kengtung in 1942; in 1943 the two states of Kengtung and Mong Pan were assigned to Thailand, and they were returned in August 1945.

摩鹿加.note: The Spice Islands. Ambon was the home of the Ambonese soldiers of the Dutch East Indies colonial army; Ternate and Tidore were old sultanates. They fell in 1942; US forces landed on Morotai in September 1944.

文莱.note: A sultanate; a British protectorate from 1888, with a British Resident from 1906. Oil was discovered at Seria in 1929. Occupied by Japanese troops in December 1941; Australian forces landed and recovered it in June 1945.

新伊大都督府.note: The New Army in Ili rose on 7 January 1912 and killed the Ili General Zhirui; on the 8th it set up the Xin-Yi Grand Military Governorate, with Guangfu as military governor and Yang Zuanxu as commander-in-chief. Advancing east, it was locked in a stalemate with the Qing forces of Dihua at Jinghe and Wusu; in summer 1912 it made peace with Yang Zengxin and was merged into Xinjiang Province.

新几内亚.note: The part of former German New Guinea south of the equator; occupied by Australian forces in 1914 and a League of Nations mandate from May 1921, with its seat at Rabaul (moved to Lae in 1941). Japanese troops took Rabaul in January 1942 and built it into the largest base in the South Pacific; the Allies bypassed it rather than attack it, and its surrender was accepted only in September 1945.

新桂系.note: Li Zongren, Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi unified Guangxi in 1924–1925 and joined the Nationalist Government in 1926; their Seventh Army was known as the “Steel Army” in the Northern Expedition. In 1927–1929 they controlled Hunan, Hubei and eastern Hebei at the height of their power, an important faction of the new warlords; defeated in the Chiang–Guangxi War of 1929, they withdrew to Guangxi and thereafter repeatedly opposed Chiang, joining the Guangzhou Nationalist Government in 1931 and, together with the Guangdong Clique, maintaining the semi-independence of the Southwest until 1936.

新疆.note: The provincial regime of Republican Xinjiang, long ruled autonomously by Han military governors (chairmen). Yang Zengxin took control of the government in Dihua in 1912, suppressed the Ili revolutionaries and the Gelaohui, incorporated Altay in 1919, and steered between Beijing, Soviet Russia and the princes of the various ethnic groups by “governing through non-action”; he was assassinated in July 1928. Jin Shuren succeeded him; the Hami Incident of 1931 set off war across Xinjiang, and after the “April 12” coup in Dihua in 1933 Sheng Shicai took power, driving back Ma Zhongying with Soviet help; in 1942 he turned to the KMT central government and became anti-Soviet and anti-Communist. In 1944 Sheng Shicai was transferred away, and the Three Districts Revolution broke out in the three districts of Ili, Tacheng and Ashan; in September 1949 Tao Zhiyue and Burhan Shahidi announced their uprising by circular telegram, and Xinjiang was peacefully liberated.

旁遮普.note: Capital at Lahore; a major recruiting ground of the British Indian Army, with Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus living intermingled. Delhi was separated in 1912 as a chief commissioner's province (on this map it remains part of this province). In 1919 British troops perpetrated the Amritsar Massacre. At the partition by religion in 1947 West Punjab went to Pakistan and East Punjab to India, and some ten million people migrated across the new border.

旅大.note: Lüshun and Dalian. Occupied by Soviet troops in August 1945; the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance of the same month made Lüshun a naval base shared by the two countries and Dalian a free port, with Soviet troops to be stationed there for thirty years. When Soviet troops withdrew from the Northeast in 1946 they did not leave here, and the CPC set up a Lüda administration under Soviet protection. The new treaty of February 1950 required Soviet troops to leave Lüshun by the end of 1952 at the latest; as the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea had not ended, the withdrawal was postponed in September 1952 at China's request. During Khrushchev's visit to China in October 1954 it was agreed that Soviet troops would leave by the end of May 1955, with the installations handed over to China without compensation.

日占东南亚.note: Between December 1941 and May 1942 Japanese troops occupied in turn Malaya, Singapore, the Philippines, the Dutch East Indies, Burma and the Pacific islands, calling them the “Southern Occupied Territories”. Malaya and Sumatra came under the 25th Army, Java under the 16th Army, British North Borneo under the army, and Dutch Borneo and Celebes and the islands east of it under the navy. In the name of the “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere” Japan carried out colonial plunder, seizing oil, rubber, tin and grain and conscripting forced labourers (“rōmusha”), which roused the people of each country to anti-Japanese struggle.

日占区.note: Areas of China occupied directly by the Japanese invading troops and not yet handed over to puppet regimes. With limited forces, the Japanese army mostly controlled only the cities and the lines along railways and roads, while the countryside was often an anti-Japanese guerrilla zone. Early in the occupation puppet Peace Maintenance Committees were set up locally; the areas were then handed over in turn to the Puppet North China Provisional Government, the Puppet Reformed Government and the Wang Jingwei Puppet Regime; Hainan Island, Xiamen and other places long remained under direct rule by the Japanese navy.

日占西伯利亚.note: In August 1918 Japan, in the name of a joint Allied expedition, launched armed intervention against Soviet Russia and advanced into Vladivostok; at its peak the force numbered over 70,000 and held Primorye, the Amur region and eastern Transbaikalia along the railways. After the US troops left in 1920 the Japanese stayed on, backing in turn the Primorye zemstvo government, the Merkulov brothers' Provisional Priamurye Government and Diterikhs's “Zemstvo Host”; on 25 October 1922 they were forced to evacuate Vladivostok.

日占阿留申.note: In June 1942, alongside the Midway operation, Japanese troops occupied Kiska (on the 6th) and Attu (on the 7th) to tie down US forces in the North Pacific. US forces recaptured Attu in May 1943, the garrison being almost entirely killed; on 29 July the Kiska garrison slipped away under cover of thick fog.

日本.note:
Capital: Tokyo
Polity: constitutional monarchy (Meiji Constitution) with the emperor as head of state; party cabinets took shape for a time in the Taishō era, and from the 1930s the fascist forces of the military gradually came to dominate the state, forming the Imperial Rule Assistance Association in 1940
Key figures: the three emperors Meiji, Taishō and Shōwa; Hara Takashi, Tanaka Giichi, Konoe Fumimaro, Tōjō Hideki; after the war Shidehara Kijūrō, Yoshida Shigeru
Territories seized: China's Taiwan, seized after the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895 (1895); Karafuto and the Kwantung Leased Territory, seized after the Russo-Japanese War (1905); Korea, annexed (1910); the South Seas Mandate, held after the First World War in the name of mandatory rule
Key events on this map (the aggression and expansion of Japanese imperialism): annexed Korea in 1910; in 1914 seized Germany's possessions in Shandong and the Pacific, and the next year presented China with the Twenty-One Demands, aimed at subjugating China; in 1918–1922 sent troops to Siberia in armed intervention against Soviet Russia; in 1931 launched the September 18 Incident and set up Puppet Manchukuo; in 1937 launched its full-scale war of aggression against China; in December 1941 made a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, starting the Pacific War, and occupied Southeast Asia and the western Pacific; in August 1945, after the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war on Japan, it announced its unconditional surrender on the 15th and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September. Thereafter it was occupied by the United States alone and lost all its colonies; a new constitution was promulgated in 1946. In September 1951, with China excluded by the United States, the one-sided San Francisco Peace Treaty with Japan (which the government of the People's Republic of China declared it would not recognize) and the Japan–US Security Treaty were signed; the peace treaty came into force on 28 April 1952 and Japan regained its sovereignty, and on the same day it signed the so-called “Japan–Taiwan Treaty” with the Taiwan authorities. In July 1954 the Defense Agency and the Ground, Maritime and Air Self-Defense Forces were established.

日本本土.note: Japan proper: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku, plus islands such as Okinawa, the Kurils and the Bonins, organized into prefectures and the Hokkaido Agency; in 1943 Karafuto too was incorporated into the “inner territories”. From September 1945 it was occupied by the United States alone in the name of Allied General Headquarters (GHQ), which kept the emperor and the Japanese government and ruled indirectly; the Ryukyus and the Bonins were handed to US forces, and the Kurils went to the Soviet Union. The one-sided San Francisco Peace Treaty was signed in September 1951 and took effect on 28 April 1952, ending the occupation and restoring sovereignty; the Tokara Islands were returned in February 1952 and the Amami Islands in December 1953, while Okinawa and the Bonins remained under US administration.

旧桂系.note: The Guangxi warlord group headed by Lu Rongting. Lu Rongting began as a roving disbanded soldier, became provincial military commander of Guangxi in the late Qing and military governor of Guangxi in the early Republic. In 1916 he joined the National Protection War and gained Guangdong, forming a combined Guangdong–Guangxi bloc; in 1917 he joined the Constitution Protection Movement under the banner of “Guangdong-Guangxi self-rule” but sidelined Sun Yat-sen, and in 1918 reorganized the Military Government and took control of politics in Guangzhou, causing the Constitution Protection Movement to fail. In 1920 he was driven out of Guangdong by Chen Jiongming's Guangdong Army; in 1921 the Guangdong Army invaded Guangxi and Lu Rongting fled. In 1923 Lu Rongting returned to Nanning and rose again; in 1924 he was besieged in Guilin by Shen Hongying and then attacked by Li Zongren and Huang Shaohong, stepping down in October. The Old Guangxi Clique was finished, and the New Guangxi Clique rose in its place.

晋冀鲁豫.note: From winter 1937 Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping's 129th Division of the Eighth Route Army opened up the Taihang, Taiyue and Southern Hebei anti-Japanese base areas, later extending into the Hebei-Shandong-Henan area; in July 1941 the Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan Border Region Government was established (based around Shexian). The Eighth Route Army headquarters was based here for a long time; in 1948 it was merged with Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei into the North China Liberated Area.

晋北自治政府.note: A puppet regime set up at Datong with the backing of Japanese forces on 15 October 1937, with Xia Gong as supreme commissioner, governing thirteen counties of northern Shanxi including Datong, Shuoxian, Hunyuan and Lingqiu. Part of the Puppet Mengjiang United Committee, it was merged into the Puppet Mengjiang United Autonomous Government in September 1939.

晋察冀.note: In November 1937 Nie Rongzhen, with part of the Eighth Route Army's 115th Division, set up the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Military Region at Wutai, and in January 1938 the Border Region Provisional Administrative Committee was established (based at Fuping): the first anti-Japanese base area behind enemy lines. It spanned the mountains of northeastern Shanxi, southern Chahar and western Hebei and the central Hebei plain; central Hebei suffered heavily in the Japanese May First Great “Mopping-up” of 1942. In 1948 it was merged with Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan into the North China Liberated Area.

晋系.note: The Shanxi warlord group headed by Yan Xishan. Yan Xishan helped lead the Taiyuan Uprising in 1911 and became military governor of Shanxi, adding the civil governorship in 1917; he kept to himself under the slogan of “protecting the borders and pacifying the people”, carried out the Six Policies and Three Undertakings and the village system, and styled Shanxi a “model province”. He mostly stayed neutral in the wars among the Beiyang warlords, joined the attack on the Guominjun in 1926, changed flags in June 1927 to become Northern Commander-in-Chief of the National Revolutionary Army, and in 1928 gained Beiping and Tianjin, Chahar and Suiyuan. Defeated in the Central Plains War of 1930, he stepped down, returning in 1932 as director of the Taiyuan Pacification Headquarters. During the War of Resistance most of Shanxi fell to the enemy, and Yan Xishan held southwestern Shanxi; he left before the liberation of Taiyuan in April 1949, later became president of the Executive Yuan of the KMT government, and retreated to Taiwan with the KMT authorities.

晋绥.note: In winter 1937 He Long and Guan Xiangying led the Eighth Route Army's 120th Division in opening up an anti-Japanese base area in northwestern Shanxi, fighting side by side with the Shanxi New Army; after the Western Shanxi Incident in early 1940 the Northwestern Shanxi Administrative Office (based at Xingxian) was set up, and the area was later called the Shanxi-Suiyuan Border Region. It spanned northwestern Shanxi and the Daqing Mountains of Suiyuan, forming the northeastern shield of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region.

暹罗.note:
Capital: Bangkok
Polity: Chakri dynasty. After the People's Party coup of 24 June 1932, a constitutional monarchy, with real power held in turn by Phraya Phahon and Luang Phibun (1938–1944 and from 1948)
The only country in Southeast Asia not reduced to a colony; in 1909 it ceded Kedah and three other Malay states to Britain. Entered the First World War in 1917. Renamed Thailand in June 1939; in the Franco-Thai War of 1941 it gained Battambang, Siem Reap and the Lao lands west of the Mekong; in December that year it allied with Japan, and in 1943 it also received the four northern Malay states and two Shan states. In September 1945 it briefly reverted to the name Siam and returned all these gains, becoming Thailand again in May 1949. The navy's Manhattan Rebellion of June 1951 failed; in September 1954 it signed the US-engineered Manila Pact (Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty), and the following year the headquarters of the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization was set up in Bangkok.

朝鲜.note: Korea (under Japanese occupation): on 29 August 1910 the Japan–Korea Annexation Treaty, which Japan had forced Korea to sign, was promulgated; Japan annexed Korea and the Korean Empire came to an end. In October the Government-General of Korea was set up in Keijo, its governors-general drawn from army generals and navy admirals, and colonial rule was imposed. After the Korean people's anti-Japanese March First Movement of 1919 Japan switched to “cultural rule”; at the end of the 1930s it forced through imperialization and the adoption of Japanese-style names, and in the last years of the war it conscripted labourers and soldiers on a massive scale. With Japan's surrender in August 1945 Korea was divided at the 38th parallel into Soviet and US occupation zones.

朝鲜民主主义人民共和国.note:
Capital: Pyongyang (the government withdrew north to Kanggye in October–December 1950)
Polity: people's republic led by the Workers' Party of Korea; Premier Kim Il Sung
In February 1946, under Soviet occupation, the Provisional People's Committee for North Korea was set up and carried out land reform; the state was founded on 9 September 1948, and Soviet troops withdrew at the end of that year. The Korean civil war broke out on 25 June 1950, and the Korean People's Army reached the Nakdong River in August; after the US Incheon landing it withdrew north; in October the Chinese People's Volunteers entered Korea to resist US aggression and aid Korea, and Pyongyang was recovered in December. In January 1951 the Chinese and Korean forces took Seoul again, withdrawing in March; thereafter the front was locked in stalemate around the 38th parallel for two years, while the North's cities and industrial facilities were bombed continuously by the US Air Force. The Armistice Agreement was signed on 27 July 1953, placing the Kaesong and Ongjin areas in the North; after the war the country was rebuilt with Soviet and Chinese aid, and the Volunteers had all withdrawn by 1958.

李弥部.note: Remnants of the KMT 8th and 26th Armies, driven out of Yunnan by the People's Liberation Army in early 1950, fled into Burma; from July they made Mong Hsat in the Shan States their headquarters, with Li Mi as commander-in-chief, and, supplied by the Taiwan authorities and the US Central Intelligence Agency, expanded into the so-called “Yunnan Anti-Communist National Salvation Army”. In May and July 1951 they twice invaded Gengma and other places in Yunnan but were soon driven back. In 1953 Burma took the matter to the United Nations; from November 1953 to May 1954 several thousand officers, men and dependants were evacuated via Thailand to Taiwan, while the rest remained on the Yunnan–Burma border.

杨森.note: Originally a subordinate commander in Liu Xiang's Second Army. Defeated in the War of the First and Second Armies in 1922, he fled to Yichang and went over to Wu Peifu; in 1923 he returned to Sichuan with Zhili Clique reinforcements, entered Chengdu in February 1924 and became Military Superintendent of Sichuan in May. In July 1925 he launched the “War of Unification”, met a joint counter-attack by Liu Xiang, Yuan Zuming and others, and was driven out of Sichuan in September.

果阿.note: Portugal's colonies in India, Goa, Damão and Diu, with the capital at Nova Goa (Panjim), plus the inland enclaves of Dadra and Nagar Haveli east of Damão (seized in July–August 1954 by volunteers seeking union with India). After India's independence Portugal refused to give them up, ruling until December 1961, when Indian troops moved in.

柬埔寨.note: A protectorate under the Norodom royal house, with its capital at Phnom Penh. Battambang and Siem Reap were recovered from Siam in 1907, ceded again under duress to Thailand in 1941 and returned in December 1946. In November 1949 it became the Kingdom of Cambodia within the French Union. In 1953 Sihanouk launched the “Royal Crusade for Independence”; on 9 November France handed over full military, police and judicial powers and Cambodia became fully independent; the Geneva Accords designated no regroupment zone in Cambodia.

柬埔寨王国.note:
Capital: Phnom Penh
Polity: monarchy; King Sihanouk, with Son Ngoc Thanh as prime minister from August
Proclaimed “independence” on 13 March 1945 after the Japanese coup. After Japan's surrender British and French troops reached Phnom Penh in October; Son Ngoc Thanh was arrested, and France restored its colonial rule (the protectorate).

格鲁吉亚.note:
Capital: Tiflis (Tbilisi)
Polity: democratic republic established on 26 May 1918, governed by the Mensheviks
Key figures: Noe Zhordania
Key events: relied at first on German protection, and British troops moved in at the end of 1918; controlled Ardahan and Artvin in 1919 and took over Batum in July 1920; in February–March 1921 the Red Army fought its way in and Soviet Georgia was established, joining the Transcaucasian Federation in 1922 and becoming a union republic in December 1936.

桦太.note: Karafuto: by the Russo-Japanese Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905 Japan took Sakhalin Island south of 50°N; the Karafuto Agency was set up in 1907, and in 1908 its seat moved from Odomari to Toyohara; the economy rested on fishing, forestry, papermaking and coal mining. Incorporated into the “inner territories” in 1943. Captured by Soviet troops in August 1945 and declared annexed by the Soviet Union in February 1946.

武汉国民政府.note:
At the end of 1926 the Nationalist Government moved north from Guangzhou and began work in Wuhan on New Year's Day 1927; Wang Jingwei headed it after returning to China in April. It was the Nationalist Government of KMT–CPC cooperation.
Capital: Wuhan (Hankou).
In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek launched the April 12 Counter-revolutionary Coup and set up a separate Nanjing Nationalist Government, splitting Nanjing from Wuhan; in May Wuhan continued the Northern Expedition and fought bloody battles with the Fengtian Army in Henan, but was soon isolated by the Horse Day Incident and Feng Yuxiang's turn towards Nanjing. On 15 July the Wang Jingwei clique carried out its “purge of Communists”, and the Great Revolution failed. In September the Nanjing and Wuhan governments merged, ending the Wuhan Nationalist Government; Tang Shengzhi defied orders while holding Hunan and Hubei, and was defeated by the Western Expedition Army in November.

比哈尔.note: Separated from Bengal in April 1912, with its capital at Patna; when Orissa was split off in April 1936 it was renamed Bihar Province. In 1917 Gandhi launched the Champaran movement here; it was struck by the great earthquake of 1934.

汉志.note:
Capital: Mecca
Polity: kingdom of the Hashemite family
Key figures: Sharif Hussein (1916–1924), Ali (1924–1925); Hussein's sons Faisal and Abdullah
Key events: in 1915–1916 Hussein corresponded with McMahon, the British High Commissioner in Egypt, and in June 1916 he launched the Arab Revolt, proclaiming himself king at the end of the year; in March 1924 he proclaimed himself caliph; that autumn Ibn Saud attacked, Mecca was lost in October and Hussein abdicated; Medina and Jeddah surrendered in December 1925, and the kingdom came to an end.

江苏讨袁军.note: On 15 July 1913 Huang Xing entered Nanjing and forced Cheng Dequan to declare Jiangsu independent; after Huang Xing left Nanjing on the 29th, He Haiming seized Nanjing again in August and declared independence, resisting the siege by Zhang Xun and Feng Guozhang until the city fell on 1 September.

汪伪.note:
Seat: Nanjing
Polity: a puppet central regime set up by the Wang Jingwei clique with Japanese backing in the name of a “return of the capital”, usurping the name of the KMT and the Blue Sky, White Sun and a Wholly Red Earth flag (at first with an added yellow triangular pennant reading “Peace, Anti-Communism, National Construction”)
Key figures: Wang Jingwei, Chen Gongbo, Zhou Fohai
Key events: established on 30 March 1940, absorbing the Puppet Reformed Government and nominally governing the Puppet North China Political Council; in November it signed the traitorous Treaty concerning Basic Relations between Japan and China with Japan; in January 1943 it declared war on Britain and the United States and “recovered” the concessions; in November 1944 Wang Jingwei died in Japan and Chen Gongbo became acting head; it announced its dissolution on 16 August 1945.

沈鸿英.note: A general of the Old Guangxi Clique, defeated in the Guangdong–Guangxi War of 1921, he retreated into Hunan and Jiangxi. At the end of 1922 he joined the campaign against Chen Jiongming; in April 1923 the Beijing Government appointed him Military Superintendent of Guangdong, and he rose in the northern outskirts of Guangzhou to attack the Generalissimo's Headquarters, but was defeated and withdrew to northern Guangxi, holding Guilin and Liuzhou. In 1924 he besieged Lu Rongting, and in early 1925 he was defeated by the New Guangxi Clique.

沙捞越.note: The hereditary domain of the “White Rajahs” of the English Brooke family; a British protectorate from 1888, with its seat at Kuching; oil was produced at Miri. Occupied by Japanese troops in December 1941; in July 1946 the third Rajah ceded sovereignty to Britain and it became a Crown colony.

沙特.note:
Capital: Riyadh
Polity: monarchy of the House of Saud, which expanded with the help of the Wahhabi movement and the Ikhwan tribal forces
Key figures: Abdulaziz Ibn Saud
Key events: restored Saudi rule at Riyadh in 1902; took Hasa in 1913; came under British protection by the Treaty of Darin in 1915; took the title Sultan of Nejd in 1921 and destroyed the Rashidis in November; took Hejaz in 1924–1925 and became King of Hejaz in 1926; by the Treaty of Jeddah of 1927 Britain recognized its full independence; put down the Ikhwan revolt in 1929–1930; adopted the name Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on 23 September 1932; defeated Yemen in 1934; oil discovered in 1938; in August 1952 sent men to occupy the Buraimi Oasis, provoking a dispute with British-protected Abu Dhabi and Muscat; Ibn Saud died in November 1953 and was succeeded by his eldest surviving son Saud.

沪军都督府.note: The Shanghai Uprising broke out on 3 November 1911; the next day the insurgents took the Jiangnan Arsenal, and Chen Qimei became Shanghai military governor. Shanghai was the financial and press centre of the revolutionary camp, and the North–South peace talks were held here.

法国.note:
Capital: Paris (the Vichy government at Vichy, 1940–1944)
Polity: Third Republic → Vichy France (1940.07–1944.08) → Provisional Government → Fourth Republic (1946.10)
In Asia: French Indochina (Tonkin, Annam, Cochinchina, Laos and Cambodia, with the Governor-General at Hà Nội), the leased territory of Guangzhouwan, five trading posts in India (Pondichéry and others), and concessions in Shanghai and elsewhere; after the First World War it also received mandates over Syria and Lebanon. After metropolitan France fell in 1940, the Vichy authorities were forced to let Japanese troops into northern Vietnam (September) and southern Vietnam (July 1941), and after the Franco-Thai War ceded territory to Thailand; in March 1945 a Japanese coup ended French rule. After the war France returned to Indochina to restore colonial rule, launched a full-scale war against the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in December 1946, and in 1949 turned instead to making the State of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia three “Associated States” of the French Union. In October–November 1953 it recognized the full independence of Laos and Cambodia; after its crushing defeat in the Điện Biên Phủ Campaign in May 1954, agreement was reached at the Geneva Conference in July and France withdrew from northern Vietnam; in November of the same year the four territories of French India were de facto transferred to India.

浙军政府.note: The New Army rose in Hangzhou on 5 November 1911 and chose Tang Shouqian as military governor; Jiang Zungui and Zhu Rui later governed Zhejiang in turn. The Zhejiang Army joined the Jiangsu-Zhejiang Allied Army in taking Nanjing. In April 1916 Zhejiang declared independence; in May Lü Gongwang became military governor and joined the National Protection side.

海南防卫.note: In April 1949 the KMT government set up the Hainan Special Region with Chen Jitang as chief executive; after the liberation of Guangzhou the remnants of the KMT forces fell back to hold Hainan, and in December Xue Yue became commander-in-chief of Hainan Defence, deploying the “Boling Line” around the island. The Qiongya Column held out in its Wuzhi Mountains base area. In the Hainan Island Campaign of March–May 1950, Haikou was liberated on 23 April and the whole of Hainan Island on 1 May.

海峡殖民地.note: A British Crown colony with its seat at Singapore, comprising Penang, Malacca and Singapore, and from 1907 also Labuan. Occupied by Japanese troops in February 1942; dissolved in April 1946, when Penang and Malacca joined the Malayan Union and Singapore became a separate Crown colony.

海得拉巴.note:
Capital: Hyderabad
Polity: Muslim princely state under the hereditary rule of the Nizam; the largest and richest princely state of British India, with a mostly Hindu population
Key figures: the seventh Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan
Key events: Berar leased to Britain in perpetuity from 1903; at the 1947 partition it refused to join either India or Pakistan, concluding a standstill agreement with India in November while the Razakar militia operated within its borders; in the Indian army's Operation Polo of 13–18 September 1948 the Nizam surrendered and the state was incorporated into India.

海陆丰.note: The peasant-movement base area of Haifeng and Lufeng in Guangdong led by Peng Pai. After two uprisings in April and September 1927, soviet governments were set up in the two counties in November, among the earliest county-level soviets in the country, carrying out the agrarian revolution; in February–March 1928 they were overrun by the KMT's Guangdong forces, and the remaining forces turned to guerrilla warfare in the mountains.

清.note:
Capital: Beijing. The Xuantong Emperor Puyi was on the throne, with Prince Chun, Zaifeng, as regent. The Qing government pursued the “New Policies” and “preparation for constitutional government”; in May 1911 it formed the “Royal Cabinet” and proclaimed the “nationalization of railways”, provoking the Railway Protection Movement. After the Wuchang Uprising the provinces declared independence one after another, and the Qing court recalled Yuan Shikai as prime minister of the cabinet; on 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu issued the edict of abdication. Qing rule came to an end, and with it the feudal autocratic monarchy of more than two thousand years.
Territory: the eighteen provinces inside the Great Wall, the Three Northeastern Provinces and Xinjiang, with Inner and Outer Mongolia, Qinghai and Xizang as dependencies; Taiwan, Hong Kong and other places had already been seized or forcibly leased by the powers.

湘军.note: The provincial army of Republican Hunan. In the Constitution Protection period it was led by Tan Yankai and Cheng Qian, fighting the Beiyang Army for Hunan in 1917–1918 and falling back to southern Hunan. In 1920 it drove out Zhang Jingyao, and Tan Yankai proclaimed Hunan self-government; in November of that year Zhao Hengti drove Tan out, promulgated a provincial constitution in 1922 and followed the federation of autonomous provinces, standing on his own between North and South; in 1921 he was defeated in the expedition to aid Hubei and lost Yuezhou, and in 1923 he drove back Tan Yankai. In 1926 Tang Shengzhi overthrew Zhao and went over to the Guangzhou Nationalist Government, while Ye Kaixin's forces attached themselves to Wu Peifu; after the Northern Expedition the various units of the Hunan Army were incorporated into the National Revolutionary Army. After 1928 Hunan was governed by Lu Diping and He Jian, He Jian holding Hunan until 1937.

湘军政府.note: Established after the New Army uprising in Changsha on 22 October 1911, with the revolutionaries Jiao Dafeng and Chen Zuoxin as military governor and deputy military governor; on the 31st both were killed in a mutiny instigated by the constitutionalists, and the constitutionalist Tan Yankai succeeded them. The Hunan Army then went to the aid of Hubei and took part in the Defence of Hanyang.

湘赣苏区.note: The continuation of the Jinggangshan Revolutionary Base Area. In October 1927 Mao Zedong led the troops of the Autumn Harvest Uprising up Jinggangshan; after the Jinggangshan rendezvous of 1928 the armed independent regime of workers and peasants on the Hunan–Jiangxi border took shape. After the Red Fourth Army left the mountains in 1929, Yongxin, Lianhua, Ninggang and other places held out, and in October 1931 Hunan-Jiangxi Province was established, centred on Yongxin. In August 1934 the Red Sixth Army Group set out from here on its Western March.

湘鄂川黔苏区.note: Opened up by the Red Second and Sixth Army Groups (He Long, Ren Bishi, Guan Xiangying, Xiao Ke) in November 1934 in the Yongshun, Dayong and Sangzhi area of western Hunan, with the provincial Party committee based at Tawo. Once established it tied down large numbers of KMT forces in Hunan and Hubei, supporting the Long March of the Central Red Army; in 1935 it won successive victories at Chenjiahe, Zhongbao and Banliyuan, and on 19 November of that year broke out from Liujiaping in Sangzhi to begin the Long March.

湘鄂西苏区.note: The Hunan-Hubei border and Honghu base areas opened up by He Long and Zhou Yiqun. In July 1930 the Red Fourth and Sixth Armies joined forces at Gong'an to form the Red Second Army Group; the soviet area spanned more than ten counties on both banks of the Yangtze River, centred on Zhoulaozui and Qujiawan in Jianli. After defeat in the fourth counter-“encirclement” campaign in 1932, the Red Third Army moved to the Hunan-Hubei-Sichuan-Guizhou border.

湘鄂赣苏区.note: The base area on the borders of Hunan, Hubei and Jiangxi opened up by Peng Dehuai and Huang Gonglüe after the Pingjiang Uprising of 1928, including the counties of Pingjiang, Liuyang, Xiushui, Tonggu and Wanzai, Yangxin in southeastern Hubei, and others. In 1930 the Red Third Army Group struck out from here and captured Changsha; the Hunan-Hubei-Jiangxi Provincial Soviet was established in 1931, and guerrilla warfare continued until the outbreak of the War of Resistance.

滇桂客军.n: Yunnan and Guangxi Armies (Yang Ximin, Liu Zhenhuan)
滇桂客军.note: Yang Ximin's Yunnan Army and Liu Zhenhuan's Guangxi Army, which came east from Guangxi at Sun Yat-sen's call at the end of 1922 as the Western Route Anti-Rebel Army and drove Chen Jiongming out of Guangzhou in January 1923. They then entrenched themselves in Guangzhou, seizing control of tax revenue, opium and gambling; in June 1925 they colluded with Duan Qirui and Tang Jiyao to rebel, and were put down by the Whampoa cadet army, the Guangdong Army and others.

滇系.note: The Yunnan warlord group headed by Tang Jiyao. In 1915 Tang Jiyao and Cai E launched the National Protection War, and the Yunnan Army's power extended into Sichuan, Guizhou and Guangxi; in 1917 Tang Jiyao formed the National Pacification Army to join the Constitution Protection Movement, and the Yunnan troops stationed in Sichuan contended with the Sichuan Army for Sichuan until 1920. In 1921 Gu Pinzhen drove Tang out, but Tang Jiyao returned in 1922, advocating a federation of autonomous provinces and standing apart from both North and South; in 1925 he attacked Guangxi and was defeated by the New Guangxi Clique. In 1927 Long Yun and others staged the “February 6 Coup”; Tang Jiyao fell from power and died of illness, and Long Yun ruled Yunnan until 1945. During the nationwide War of Resistance Yunnan was part of the great rear area; in October 1945 Chiang Kai-shek reorganized the Yunnan provincial government by force, and Long Yun was dismissed and transferred away.

澳大利亚.note:
Capital: Canberra (Parliament sat in Melbourne before 1927)
Polity: British dominion; federal parliamentary system
Took over British New Guinea in 1906, renaming it the Territory of Papua; occupied German New Guinea in September 1914 and from 1921 administered it as a League of Nations mandate, and also administered Nauru jointly with Britain and New Zealand. In 1942–1945 Australian forces fought in Papua, New Guinea and Borneo. This map extends only to 11°S, so of the mainland only Cape York appears.

烟台军政府.note: Yantai rose on 12 November 1911 and set up a military sub-government. Shandong's independence was soon revoked, but Yantai remained in the hands of the revolutionary army; in January 1912 southern reinforcements advanced from here to take Dengzhou and Huangxian. Abolished after North and South were united.

热河都统.note: The Rehe Special Region, whose lieutenant-governor sat at Chengde, governing the counties of Rehe Circuit and the Josotu and Ju Ud leagues. In 1913–1921 the Yi Army veteran Jiang Guiti was lieutenant-governor, belonging to neither the Zhili nor the Anhui clique; thereafter the office changed hands with the fortunes of Zhili and Fengtian.

熊克武.note: A Tongmenghui member and commander of the 5th Division of the Sichuan Army. At the end of 1917 he joined the Yunnan and Guizhou armies in the Constitution Protection cause, and in March 1918 was appointed military governor of Sichuan by the Military Government; in 1920 he lost Chengdu to Lü Chao and the Yunnan Army, but soon allied with Liu Xiang and Liu Cunhou to drive out the Yunnan and Guizhou armies. In 1923 Sun Yat-sen made him commander-in-chief of the Sichuan Anti-Rebel Army; defeated by Yang Sen and Liu Xiang in early 1924, he led his troops through Guizhou into Hunan and Guangdong.

爪哇.note: The core of the Dutch East Indies, with most of its population and the Governor-General's seat at Batavia. Dutch forces surrendered to the Japanese army on 8 March 1942. Indonesia proclaimed independence in Djakarta in August 1945; the Javanese cities later reoccupied by the Dutch colonialists and the areas occupied in the two colonial wars (the so-called “police actions”) are also shown under this unit.

特拉凡哥尔.note: Two Hindu princely states on the Malabar Coast at India's southern tip, with the highest literacy in all India. In June 1947 the Dewan of Travancore proclaimed independence, but at the end of July the Maharaja agreed to join India; the two states merged in 1949.

特鲁西尔.note: The sheikhdoms of Sharjah, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain and Ras al-Khaimah. In 1853 they concluded the Perpetual Maritime Truce with Britain (hence the name “Trucial States”), and after the exclusive agreements of 1892 their foreign affairs were handled by Britain.

琉球美军.note: After the Battle of Okinawa in April–June 1945 US forces occupied Okinawa Island and set up a military government; after Japan's surrender the Miyako, Yaeyama and Amami islands also came under US forces. In January 1946 a GHQ directive separated the Ryukyu Islands south of 30°N (including the Tokara Islands) from Japanese administration and placed them under US military rule. In December 1950 this was replaced by the United States Civil Administration of the Ryukyu Islands, and in April 1952 the Government of the Ryukyu Islands was set up; Article 3 of the San Francisco Peace Treaty provided for continued US administration, with Japan retaining “residual sovereignty”. The Tokara Islands were returned to Japan in February 1952 and the Amami Islands on 25 December 1953; Okinawa was returned only in 1972.

琼崖.note: The Hainan Island base area led by the CPC Qiongya Special Committee. After the Qiongya armed uprising of September 1927, the Lingshui County Soviet Government was set up in November; after setbacks in winter 1928 the forces fell back to hold Muruishan, in 1930 rebuilt the Qiongya Soviet and the Red Army Independent Division, and in 1932 again faced a KMT “encirclement” campaign. During the War of Resistance the Qiongya Column was formed, which kept up armed struggle until the liberation of Hainan Island in 1950.

瑙鲁.note: A phosphate island, formerly German; occupied by Australian forces in November 1914, it was from 1920 a mandate held jointly by Britain, Australia and New Zealand and administered by Australia. Japanese troops occupied it in August 1942 and forcibly deported islanders to Truk.

甘军.note: The provincial government and army of Gansu in the Beiyang period. Zhang Guangjian (Anhui Clique) was military governor of Gansu in 1914–1920, succeeded by Lu Hongtao in 1921–1925; within the province, garrison commissioners such as Ma Qi (Xining), Ma Fuxiang and Ma Hongbin (Ningxia), Ma Tingxiang (Liangzhou), Ma Lin (Ganzhou), Kong Fanjin (southern Gansu) and Zhang Zhaojia (eastern Gansu) each held a share, known as the “Eight Garrisons”. In 1925 Liu Yufen of the Guominjun entered Gansu, and the garrisons either submitted or were wiped out; after 1928 Gansu, Qinghai and Ningxia became separate provinces, the Ma warlords of Hehuang grew powerful, and Gansu's politics long remained unsettled.

皖军政府.note: Anqing declared independence on 8 November 1911, and the governor Zhu Jiabao briefly served as military governor; the Huaishang Army separately held Shouzhou and Yingzhou. In 1912 Sun Yujun and Bai Wenwei governed Anhui in turn; in 1913 Bai Wenwei joined the Second Revolution and was defeated.

皖系.note: The faction of the Beiyang warlords headed by Duan Qirui, a native of Hefei, Anhui, backed by Japan. After Yuan Shikai's death Duan Qirui controlled the Beijing Government as premier; in 1917 he crushed the Zhang Xun Restoration and pursued a policy of “unification by force”, used the Japanese Nishihara Loans to raise and train the War Participation Army (Frontier Defence Army), and fostered the Anfu Parliament, with Xu Shuzheng as his right-hand man. Its territory comprised Anhui, Zhejiang, Fujian, Shandong and Shaanxi, with Hunan as well in 1918–1920. In the Zhili–Anhui War of 1920 it collapsed within five days and Duan stepped down; the remnant under Lu Yongxiang held Zhejiang until 1924. In 1924–1926 Duan Qirui rose again as Provisional Chief Executive, wavering between the Fengtian Clique and the Guominjun; he fled in April 1926, and the Anhui Clique disappeared with him.

直系.note: The faction of the Beiyang warlords headed by Feng Guozhang and Cao Kun, named after Zhili, the native province of both, and backed by Britain and the United States. Feng Guozhang was acting president in 1917–1918; after his death in 1919 Cao Kun and Wu Peifu led the clique, holding Zhili, Jiangsu, Jiangxi and Hubei and later gaining Henan and Shaanxi. Victorious in the Zhili–Anhui War of 1920 and the First Zhili–Fengtian War of 1922, it controlled the Beijing Government alone, and in 1923 Cao Kun bribed his way to the presidency. It collapsed after Feng Yuxiang's Beijing Coup and its defeat in the Second Zhili–Fengtian War in 1924; Wu Peifu rose again at Hankou in 1925 with the Allied Anti-Rebel Army, and Sun Chuanfang set up a separate Five-Province Allied Army; in 1926–1927 both were routed in turn by the National Revolutionary Army on the Northern Expedition.

直鲁联军.note: The troops commanded by the Fengtian Clique warlords Zhang Zongchang (Shandong) and Chu Yupu (Zhili), formed at the end of 1925 and known for their White Russian mercenaries and armoured trains. In 1927 they moved south to hold Xuzhou and Bengbu, as part of the Anguojun system; in the Second Northern Expedition of 1928 they retreated step by step, and the remnants, having fallen back to Luandong, were caught between the National Revolutionary Army and the Fengtian Army and disarmed in September.

石友三.note: A typical figure of the wars among the new warlords, Shi Yousan came from the Northwestern Army and was notorious for repeatedly changing sides: in May 1929 he went over to Chiang with Han Fuju; in December he turned against Chiang at Pukou and shelled Nanjing; in the Central Plains War he sided with Yan and Feng, then in September went over to Zhang Xueliang, stationed at Shunde in southern Hebei. In July 1931, commissioned by the Guangzhou Nationalist Government, he attacked north towards Baoding, and was defeated in early August.

福建人民政府.n: People's Revolutionary Government of the Chinese Republic
福建人民政府.note:
Capital: Fuzhou (1933.11–1934.01)
Polity: People's Revolutionary Government of the Chinese Republic, chaired by Li Jishen; it discarded the Blue Sky with a White Sun flag and the KMT, and organized a new Productive People's Party.
Key figures: Li Jishen, Chen Mingshu, Jiang Guangnai, Cai Tingkai, Eugene Chen.
Key events: the 19th Route Army, transferred to Fujian after the January 28 Songhu Resistance, was dissatisfied with Chiang Kai-shek's policy of “internal pacification before resisting foreign aggression”; in October 1933 it concluded a preliminary anti-Japanese, anti-Chiang agreement with the Red Army, and on 20 November the government was proclaimed at Fuzhou, calling for resistance to Japan and opposition to Chiang; members of the Third Party and the Shenzhou Guoguang Society took part. Chiang Kai-shek sent the Central Army into Fujian from the north, taking Yanping, Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Zhangzhou in quick succession in January 1934; the 19th Route Army was reorganized, and the government collapsed after only two months.

科威特.note: A sheikhdom of the Al Sabah family. In 1899 Mubarak concluded a secret agreement with Britain, which took charge of its foreign affairs; in November 1914 Britain recognized it as an independent sheikhdom under British protection. The Uqair Conference of 1922 fixed its border with Nejd and created a Neutral Zone; the Burgan oilfield was discovered in 1938.

科布多参赞.note: Jurisdiction of the Kobdo Councillor-Amban, governing the Dörbet, Zakhchin, Myangad and other tribes of western Outer Mongolia. After Outer Mongolia's “independence” Qing troops still held the town of Kobdo; it fell on 20 August 1912, and the Councillor-Amban Purun was escorted out of the territory by the Russian consul.

穆哈梅拉.note:
Capital: Mohammerah (now Khorramshahr)
Polity: sheikhdom of the Arab Ka'b tribe, nominally part of Persia but in practice autonomous
Key figures: Sheikh Khazal
Key events: under British protection and cooperating with the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, whose Abadan refinery and pipelines lay in its territory; rose against Reza Khan in 1924, was lured into captivity in April 1925 and taken to Tehran, after which Khuzestan came under direct central rule.

突厥斯坦.note: The Governor-Generalship of Russian Turkestan, seated at Tashkent, comprising the Syr Darya, Fergana, Samarkand, Semirechye and Transcaspian oblasts. The Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Republic was established in April 1918; after the national delimitation of October 1924 it was replaced by the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic (this map continues the same unit), with its capital at Samarkand, moved to Tashkent in 1930; Karakalpakia was incorporated in 1936.

粤军.note: The Guangdong troops commanded by Chen Jiongming. In 1917 Sun Yat-sen handed twenty battalions of the civil governor's guard to Chen Jiongming, which were organized as the Guangdong Army to Aid Fujian; in 1918 it entered Fujian and held Zhangzhou and more than twenty other counties. In 1920 it returned to drive out the Guangxi Clique, and Chen Jiongming became civil governor of Guangdong and commander-in-chief of the Guangdong Army, taking Guangxi in 1921. Sun Yat-sen insisted on the Northern Expedition, while Chen Jiongming advocated a federation of autonomous provinces; on 16 June 1922 Chen Jiongming launched his rebellion, his subordinate Ye Ju shelled the presidential office, and Sun Yat-sen left Guangdong. In January 1923 Chen Jiongming was driven out of Guangzhou by the Yunnan and Guangxi armies and held the Dong River and Chaozhou–Meizhou areas in confrontation with the Generalissimo's Headquarters, while his subordinate Deng Benyin held southern Guangdong; after the two Eastern Expeditions of 1925 his army was wiped out by the National Revolutionary Army, and Chen Jiongming fled to Hong Kong. Xu Chongzhi's troops separately formed the Guangdong Army for National Construction.

粤军政府.note: Guangdong declared independence on 9 November 1911, with Hu Hanmin as military governor and Chen Jiongming as his deputy, later acting military governor. In July 1913 Chen Jiongming declared independence to campaign against Yuan; in August Guangzhou was occupied by Long Jiguang.

粤系.note: The Guangdong local power group headed by Chen Jitang. After the Northern Expedition Li Jishen governed Guangdong as commander of the 8th Route Army; in March 1929 Li was detained by Chiang Kai-shek, and Chen Jitang took over the Guangdong Army, nominally under Nanjing but in fact self-contained. In 1931 he joined the Guangzhou Nationalist Government, and thereafter ruled Guangdong as his own domain in the name of the Southwest Political Council, styled the “King of the South”; he stepped down after the failure of the Guangdong–Guangxi Incident in 1936.

红二六军团.n: Red Second and Sixth Army Groups
红二六军团.note: He Long's Red Second Army Group and Xiao Ke and Ren Bishi's Red Sixth Army Group joined forces at Muhuang in eastern Guizhou in October 1934 and opened up the Hunan-Hubei-Sichuan-Guizhou Base Area. In November 1935 they broke out and began the Long March, manoeuvring through the Wumeng Mountains; in April 1936 they crossed the Jinsha River at Shigu, and in July joined the Red Fourth Front Army at Garze, forming the Red Second Front Army.

约旦.note:
Capital: Amman
Polity: in April 1921 Britain installed Abdullah as Emir of Transjordan, which belonged to the Palestine mandate but was exempt from its Jewish national home provisions; independent as the Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan from 25 May 1946, renamed Jordan in 1949
Key figures: Abdullah I; Glubb, commander of the Arab Legion
Key events: acquired Ma'an and Aqaba from Hejaz in 1925; in 1948 the Arab Legion seized the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank of the Jordan River; armistice with Israel in April 1949; formal annexation of the West Bank in April 1950; Abdullah was assassinated in Jerusalem in July 1951 and succeeded by Talal, who was deposed by parliament in August 1952 and succeeded by Hussein.

维新政府.note:
Seat: Nanjing
Polity: a puppet regime backed by the Japanese Central China Expeditionary Army, named the “Reformed Government of the Republic of China”, with three yuan (executive, legislative and judicial) and using the Five-Coloured Flag
Key figures: Liang Hongzhi (president of the Executive Yuan), Wen Zongyao, Chen Qun
Key events: established on 28 March 1938, governing the occupied areas of the three provinces of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui and the two special municipalities of Nanjing and Shanghai, with real power in the hands of Japanese special service agencies and advisers; merged into the Wang Jingwei Puppet Nationalist Government on 30 March 1940.

缅甸国.note:
Capital: Rangoon
Polity: Japanese-backed puppet “independent state”, with Ba Maw as head of state (“Adipadi”) and prime minister, and Aung San as minister of defence
Proclaimed “independence” on 1 August 1943 and declared war on Britain and the United States; Japanese troops still garrisoned the whole country, and the two states of Kengtung and Mong Pan were separately assigned to Thailand. On 27 March 1945 Aung San led the Burma National Army in an anti-Japanese uprising; in late April Ba Maw left Rangoon with the Japanese army and fled via Moulmein to Japan, and the regime collapsed.

缅甸联邦.note:
Capital: Rangoon
Polity: parliamentary federal republic; President Sao Shwe Thaik, Prime Minister U Nu
After a long struggle by the Burmese people against British rule, and the assassination of Aung San in July 1947, Burma became independent on 4 January 1948, staying out of the Commonwealth. After independence the “White Flag” and “Red Flag” factions of the Communist Party of Burma and the Karen National Defence Organisation took up arms one after another; in 1949 Karen forces at one point closed in on Rangoon, and for a time the government controlled only the area around Rangoon, earning the name “Rangoon government”. From 1950 Li Mi's KMT remnant forces entrenched themselves in the eastern Shan States; in 1953 Burma stopped accepting US aid and took the matter to the United Nations, and in 1953–1954 part of the remnant forces were evacuated via Thailand to Taiwan.

美占太平洋.note: The Marshall, Mariana and Palau islands seized by US forces from the Japanese mandate in 1944, and the whole of the South Seas Mandate taken over after the war. In July 1947 they became the UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States, which had the right to fortify them.

美占朝鲜.note: On 8 September 1945 the US XXIV Corps landed at Incheon and accepted the Japanese surrender in Keijo the next day, dividing Korea with the Soviet troops along the 38th parallel; it set up the US Army Military Government in Korea (Hodge) and recognized neither Lyuh Woon-hyung's People's Republic of Korea nor the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea that had returned from Chongqing. Authority was handed over to the Republic of Korea in August 1948.

美国.note:
Capital: Washington
In Asia and the Pacific: bought Alaska in 1867, the western Aleutian Islands reaching to just east of Kamchatka; acquired the Philippines and Guam after the Spanish–American War of 1898, and annexed Hawaii in the same year. Put forward the “Open Door” policy towards China, took part in the intervention in Siberia in 1918–1920, and hosted the Washington Conference in 1921–1922. Declared war on Japan after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 and counter-attacked through the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, Saipan, Leyte Gulf, Iwo Jima and Okinawa, dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. After the war it occupied Japan alone under MacArthur and ruled the Ryukyu Islands, the Bonin Islands and southern Korea directly; in June 1950 it intervened militarily in the Korean civil war, assembling the so-called “UN Command” forces, and sent the Seventh Fleet to intrude into the Taiwan Strait. In September 1951 it signed the one-sided San Francisco Peace Treaty with Japan and the Japan–US Security Treaty, under which the Ryukyu and Bonin islands remained under US administration; it signed the Korean Armistice Agreement in July 1953 and the US–ROK Mutual Defense Treaty in October; in December 1954 it signed the so-called “Mutual Defense Treaty” with the Taiwan authorities.

老挝.note: Seat at Vientiane; the Kingdom of Luang Prabang in the north was a protectorate, the rest under direct French rule. In 1941 Sayaboury and Champassak west of the Mekong were ceded to Thailand; they were returned in 1946. In July 1949 it became the Kingdom of Laos within the French Union. In April 1953 the Vietnam People's Army and Pathet Lao forces advanced into Upper Laos; on 22 October the Franco-Lao Treaty recognized its full independence; the 1954 Geneva Accords had the Pathet Lao forces regroup in the two provinces of Sam Neua and Phongsaly.

联合国军占领区.note: In early October 1950 the US-led “UN Command” forces crossed the 38th parallel and took Pyongyang on the 19th; between late October and late November their spearheads reached Chosan and Hyesan on the Yalu River, carrying the flames of war to China's border. The Republic of Korea claimed sovereignty over the North, while a UN resolution placed civil administration of the North temporarily under the “UN Command”. In December they withdrew before the counter-attack of the Chinese People's Volunteers and the Korean People's Army. In March–June 1951 the “UN Command” forces crossed the 38th parallel again and held Yangyang, Sokcho and Ganseong on the east coast and the Cheorwon, Gimhwa, Hwacheon, Yanggu, Inje and Yeoncheon area in the centre; after the armistice these went to the South but remained under the military administration of the “UN Command” until administrative authority was transferred to the ROK in November 1954 (the ROK calls them the “recovered areas”).

联合省.note: Capital at Allahabad, shifting gradually to Lucknow after 1921. The most densely populated province of the Ganges plain and a stronghold of both the Congress and the Muslim League; the Nehru family lived at Allahabad. The Chauri Chaura incident of 1922 led Gandhi to call off the Non-cooperation Movement.

胶东刘珍年.note: Liu Zhennian, who came from the Zhili-Shandong Allied Army, held Yantai, Penglai, Huangxian and more than ten other counties of Jiaodong with the 21st Division, forming his own faction. In September–November 1932 he fought Han Fuju (the Han–Liu War); through Nanjing's mediation he was transferred to Zhejiang, and Jiaodong went to Han.

胶州湾.note: In November 1897 Germany used the Juye Incident as a pretext to seize it by force, and in March of the following year forced the Qing government to sign a 99-year lease; Germany built Qingdao harbour and the Qingdao–Jinan Railway. In November 1914 Japanese and British forces took Qingdao and Japan took over; the Paris Peace Conference's transfer of it to Japan sparked the patriotic May Fourth Movement, and in December 1922 it was returned to China under the treaty concluded at the Washington Conference.

舟山防卫.note: After the liberation of Shanghai and Ningbo in May 1949, Shi Jue's KMT forces fell back to hold the Zhoushan Islands, centred on Dinghai, from where they blockaded the mouth of the Yangtze River and bombed Shanghai. In the Battle of Dengbu Island in November the KMT forces held the island. On 13–16 May 1950 the KMT forces withdrew, about 120,000 men leaving for Taiwan, and the Zhoushan Islands were liberated on 19 May.

苏军占领区.note: In August 1945 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan, and the Soviet Red Army occupied Northeast China, Rehe, northern Chahar and northern Korea. In the Northeast, Soviet troops dismantled and carried off large quantities of industrial and mining equipment and tacitly allowed CPC forces into the towns and countryside, while handing the big cities over to the Nationalist Government under the treaty; they withdrew in stages in March–May 1946, keeping only Lüshun and Dalian. They left northern Korea by the end of 1948.

苏军政府.note: On 5 November 1911 the Jiangsu governor Cheng Dequan declared independence at Suzhou and made himself military governor, an example of old bureaucrats opportunistically “coming over”. The Jiangsu-Zhejiang Allied Army took Nanjing on 2 December, and the governorate later moved to Nanjing.

苏莱曼尼亚.note: The regime of the Kurdish leader Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji, centred on Sulaymaniyah. In November 1918 the British appointed him governor of the area; in May 1919 he rose and declared himself independent, but in June he was defeated, captured and exiled; in 1922 Britain brought him back to counterbalance Turkey, and in October he proclaimed himself “King of Kurdistan”; bombed by the British air force in 1923–1924, he lost Sulaymaniyah when British forces retook it in July 1924, and thereafter he held out in the mountains until 1931.

苏门答腊.note: The Medan area on the east coast was a tobacco and rubber plantation zone, and Palembang had oilfields; the people of Aceh resisted the Dutch colonialists in a long war from 1873 to 1904. After 1945 Dutch forces reoccupied Medan, Palembang and Padang and widened their occupation in the two offensives of 1947 and 1948, but Aceh remained in the Republic's hands throughout.

英占区.note: Key points occupied, mainly by British troops, around the time of the Ottoman defeat: the Gallipoli beachheads (1915), both shores of the Dardanelles (1918–1923), İzmit (1920–1921), Marash, Aintab and Urfa (1919) and Batum (1918–1920); in 1945–1947 British forces held the Dodecanese under caretaker administration.

英国.note:
Capital: London (off the map)
Polity: parliamentary constitutional monarchy, centre of the British Empire
In Asia: exercised colonial rule over British India (the Governor-General and Viceroy sat at Calcutta, moving to Delhi in 1912 and to New Delhi in 1931), and ruled directly the colonies of Ceylon, Burma, the Straits Settlements, China's Hong Kong, Aden and others; held Sikkim, Bhutan, the Maldives and the Gulf sheikhdoms as protectorates, and claimed suzerainty over the Indian princely states; after the First World War obtained mandates over Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan
Key events: defeated the Ottoman Empire in Mesopotamia and Palestine in 1914–1918; perpetrated the Amritsar Massacre in 1919, after which the Indian national movement surged, and promulgated the Government of India Act in 1935; occupied Iran together with the Soviet Union in 1941; fought Japan in 1941–1945, losing Burma and Malaya for a time; carried out the partition of India and Pakistan under the “Mountbatten Plan” in August 1947 and withdrew from Burma, Ceylon and Palestine in 1948, as its colonial system gradually disintegrated. In 1951 Iran nationalized its oil and the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company withdrew from Abadan; from 1952 Britain disputed the Buraimi Oasis with Saudi Arabia.

英属缅甸.note: Through three wars of aggression against Burma, Britain annexed the whole country to British India in 1886 as one of its provinces, with its capital at Rangoon. On 1 April 1937, under the Government of India Act 1935, it was separated from India and became a separate British Crown colony. The whole country was occupied by Japanese troops by May 1942; British forces recovered it in 1945, and Burma became independent in January 1948.

草原.note: The Akmolinsk, Semipalatinsk, Turgay and Ural oblasts. At the end of 1917 the Alash party set up the Alash Autonomy government, which wavered between Reds and Whites in the Civil War; in August 1920 the Kirghiz (i.e. Kazakh) Autonomous Republic was established, with its capital at Orenburg (off the map); in 1925 it was renamed the Kazakh Autonomous Republic and its capital moved to Kzyl-Orda, then in 1929 to Alma-Ata; in December 1936 it was raised to a union republic.

荷兰.note:
Capital: Amsterdam (government at The Hague)
Polity: constitutional monarchy, Queen Wilhelmina (1890–1948), Queen Juliana
In Asia: the Dutch East Indies (present-day Indonesia), with the Governor-General at Batavia, among the world's leading exporters of oil, rubber, tin, sugar and coffee; the colonial conquest of Aceh, Bali and the Outer Islands was completed in the early 20th century. In May 1940 the home country was occupied by Germany and the government went into exile in London; in March 1942 the Netherlands East Indies Army (KNIL) surrendered to the Japanese forces. Returning after 1945, the Dutch suppressed the Republic of Indonesia, which had declared independence, and launched two colonial wars (so-called “police actions”) in 1947 and 1948; faced with the resistance of the Indonesian people and pressure from the United States and the United Nations, they were forced to transfer sovereignty in December 1949, retaining only West New Guinea.

荷属婆罗洲.note: Pontianak in the west, Banjarmasin in the south, and the Balikpapan and Tarakan oilfields in the east. It fell in January–February 1942; Australian forces landed at Tarakan and Balikpapan in May–July 1945, and after the war it reverted to the Netherlands, which from 1946 sponsored the formation of several “autonomous states” there.

荷属新几内亚.note: Nominally under the Moluccas and largely undeveloped; Hollandia was founded in 1910. In 1942 Japanese troops took the ports of the north coast, while Merauke on the south coast stayed in Allied hands throughout; in 1944 US forces captured Hollandia and Biak. At the 1949 transfer of sovereignty the Netherlands retained this territory, leaving it for later negotiation.

菲律宾.note: Grabbed by the United States after the Spanish–American War of 1898; in 1902 the United States suppressed the resistance of the Filipino people led by the First Philippine Republic and installed a Governor-General in Manila to impose colonial rule. The Tydings–McDuffie Act of 1934 promised independence after ten years, and in November 1935 the Commonwealth was established with Quezon as president. Occupied by Japanese troops in 1942; US forces returned in October 1944, and the Philippines became independent on 4 July 1946.

菲律宾共和国.note:
Capital: Manila (Quezon City the official capital from 1948)
Polity: presidential republic; Roxas and Quirino served in turn as president
Became independent on 4 July 1946, while being forced to conclude unequal trade and military bases agreements with the United States, which kept Clark, Subic and other bases. From 1946 the Huk army led by the Communist Party of the Philippines kept up an armed struggle in central Luzon. In August 1951 a Mutual Defense Treaty was concluded with the United States; after Magsaysay became defence secretary he combined suppression with conciliation and the Huks declined; he was elected president in 1953, and Taruc surrendered in May the following year; in September 1954 the Manila Pact was signed here.

菲律宾第二共和国.note:
Capital: Manila (moved to Baguio in December 1944)
Polity: Japanese-backed puppet republic, with Laurel as president
Proclaimed “independence” on 14 October 1943 and concluded a treaty of alliance with Japan, declaring war on the United States and Britain in September 1944. After US forces landed on Leyte and Mindoro the government withdrew to Baguio in December; in March 1945 Laurel went to Japan via Taiwan, and on 17 August the government declared itself dissolved at Nara.

萨卡维.note: In January 1929 Habibullah Kalakani, a Tajik known as the “Son of the Water-Carrier”, exploiting the rebellion provoked by Amanullah's reforms, broke into Kabul and made himself emir, holding Kabul and the north. In October that year Nadir Khan took Kabul with southern tribal forces, and Kalakani was executed in November.

萨摩斯.note: An autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty from 1834, with a Christian prince appointed by the sultan; capital at Vathy (now Samos town). In November 1912, during the First Balkan War, it declared union with Greece, and it was incorporated into Greece in 1913.

葡属帝汶.note: The eastern half of Timor plus the Oecusse enclave in the west, with its seat at Dili; the boundary with the Dutch was settled in 1914. In December 1941 Dutch and Australian troops landed in disregard of Portuguese neutrality; Japanese troops occupied it in February 1942, and tens of thousands of Timorese died in the fighting and famine. Portuguese rule was restored in September 1945.

葡萄牙.note:
Capital: Lisbon
Polity: the monarchy was overthrown and a republic established in October 1910; military coup in 1926; from 1932 dictatorship by Salazar under the “New State” system
In Asia: China's Macao (gradually occupied by Portugal from the mid-16th century), Portuguese India (Goa, Damão and Diu) and Portuguese Timor. Portugal stayed neutral in the Second World War, but Timor was occupied by Dutch and Australian troops in December 1941 and by Japanese forces in February 1942, Portuguese rule resuming only in September 1945; Macao was not occupied and became a wartime transit point for refugees and goods. In July–August 1954 the inland enclaves of Dadra and Nagar Haveli in Portuguese India were seized by Indian nationalist volunteers.

蒙古联盟自治政府.note: A puppet regime set up with the backing of Japanese forces on 28 October 1937 at Guisui (renamed Houhehaote), with Prince Yun as chairman and Prince De as vice-chairman; after Prince Yun died in 1938, Prince De succeeded him. It governed the Xilin Gol, Chahar, Ulanqab and Bayan Tala leagues. Merged into the Puppet Mengjiang United Autonomous Government in September 1939.

蒙政会.note: Set up at Bailingmiao in April 1934 with the approval of the Nationalist Government, with Prince Yun as chairman and Prince De as secretary-general, governing all the leagues and banners of Inner Mongolia. As Prince De increasingly threw in his lot with the Japanese Kwantung Army, in February 1936 Nanjing set up a separate Suiyuan Mongolian Political Council (Prince Sha) to win over Ih Ju and the western part of Ulanqab, and the original council existed in name only.

蒙疆.note:
Capital: Dehua (1936) → Houhe (Guisui, 1937) → Zhangjiakou (1939–1945)
Polity: a puppet regime backed by the Japanese Kwantung Army: in May 1936 the Puppet Mongol Military Government (Prince Yun chairman, Prince De director-general); in October 1937 it became the Puppet Mongol United Autonomous Government, while in the same year the Puppet South Chahar and Puppet North Shanxi autonomous governments were set up separately, and in November the three formed the Puppet Mengjiang United Committee; in September 1939 they were merged into the Puppet Mengjiang United Autonomous Government, styled the “Mongol Autonomous State” after 1941.
Key figures: Prince De (Demchugdongrub), Li Shouxin, Prince Yun.
Key events: in December 1935 the Puppet Mongol Army seized six counties of northern Chahar; in November 1936 it invaded Suiyuan and was defeated by Fu Zuoyi's forces, and Bailingmiao was recovered; in 1937 it followed the Japanese forces in occupying Suiyuan and northern Shanxi; in August 1945 the Soviet-Mongolian forces attacked, and the puppet regime collapsed.

蜀军政府.note: Established after the Tongmenghui uprising in Chongqing on 22 November 1911, with Zhang Peijue as military governor, governing the prefectures and counties of eastern Sichuan. In February 1912 it agreed to merge with the Chengdu military government, and Zhang Peijue became deputy military governor of Sichuan.

西北解放区.note: Made up of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia and Shanxi-Suiyuan Border Regions, with the Northwest Field Army (Peng Dehuai) as its main force. In March 1947 it withdrew from Yan'an on its own initiative and fought on the move in northern Shaanxi; after the Yichuan Campaign of 1948 it went over to the counter-offensive and recovered Yan'an; it liberated Xi'an in May 1949 and Lanzhou in August, and Ningxia and Qinghai in September, while Xinjiang was peacefully liberated. In January 1950 the Northwest Military and Administrative Committee (Peng Dehuai) was set up, seated at Xi'an and governing the five provinces of Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia, Qinghai and Xinjiang. It became the Northwest Administrative Committee in November 1952; in September 1954 Ningxia Province was merged into Gansu, and at the end of the year the greater administrative region was abolished.

西北边境省.note: Separated from the Punjab by Curzon in 1901, with its capital at Peshawar; it also oversaw the Pashtun tribal areas and princely states such as Chitral. Tribal revolts were frequent, and troops were sent into Waziristan in 1919 and again in 1936–1939; Ghaffar Khan's “Red Shirts” were aligned with the Congress. In July 1947 a referendum took it to Pakistan.

西南解放区.note: In November–December 1949 the Second Field Army and part of the First Field Army advanced into Sichuan and Guizhou; Chongqing, Guiyang and Chengdu were liberated one after another, and Liu Wenhui, Deng Xihou and Pan Wenhua, together with Lu Han in Yunnan, announced their uprisings by circular telegram. The Southwest Bureau was based at Chongqing; in July 1950 the Southwest Military and Administrative Committee (chairman Liu Bocheng) was set up, governing the four administrative offices of East, West, South and North Sichuan together with Guizhou, Yunnan and Xikang. In October of that year the Qamdo Campaign liberated Qamdo, and in January 1951 the Qamdo Area People's Liberation Committee was set up. In September 1952 the four administrative offices of East Sichuan and the rest were merged into Sichuan Province, and in November the committee was renamed the Southwest Administrative Committee; in June 1954 the central authorities decided to abolish the greater administrative regions, and it was wound up in November.

西印度诸土邦.note: Baroda (Gaekwad family), the princely states of the Kathiawar peninsula, and Cutch. In 1947 the Muslim Nawab of Junagadh announced accession to Pakistan; India took over in November, and after a plebiscite the following year Junagadh was merged into India; the rest joined India.

西昌防区.note: During the war a Xichang Field Headquarters was set up at Xichang in the Ningshu area. Around the liberation of Chengdu in December 1949, Hu Zongnan flew from Chengdu to Xichang and gathered the remnants in the name of the Southwest Military and Political Chief's Office, hoping to hold the Xikang–Yunnan border region and await help. In the Xichang Campaign of March 1950 Hu Zongnan flew out on 26 March, Xichang was liberated on the 27th, and one of the last KMT strongholds on the mainland was eliminated.

西藏.note:
Seat: Lhasa. The Local Government of Xizang, in which the Dalai Lama presided over both religious and secular affairs, with the Kashag as its executive body.
In 1910 the Sichuan Army entered Lhasa and the 13th Dalai Lama fled to India; after the 1911 Revolution the Sichuan Army in Xizang mutinied, and the pro-British forces among the upper strata of Xizang launched the “expulsion of the Han”, driving the Sichuan troops out in 1912. The Dalai Lama returned to Xizang in 1913 and ran religious and secular affairs on his own authority; the Republic of China upheld its sovereignty but was unable to exercise actual jurisdiction.
In 1913–1914 Britain engineered the Simla Conference, and through a secret exchange of notes between Britain and Xizang concocted the illegal “McMahon Line”, which the Chinese government never recognized; thereafter the Tibetan army and the Sichuan Frontier army clashed from time to time in Kham.
In October 1950 the People's Liberation Army fought the Qamdo Campaign, and the 14th Dalai Lama assumed power ahead of time and left for Yadong. On 23 May 1951 representatives of the Local Government of Xizang signed in Beijing the Agreement of the Central People's Government and the Local Government of Xizang on Measures for the Peaceful Liberation of Xizang (17-Article Agreement); Xizang was peacefully liberated, and the Local Government of Xizang came under the unified leadership of the Central People's Government, the existing political system and the status of the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama remaining unchanged and the Kashag continuing to manage internal affairs. The Dalai Lama returned to Lhasa in August, and the People's Liberation Army entered Lhasa in October; in 1952 the 10th Panchen Lama returned to Xigaze, and in 1954 the Xikang–Xizang and Qinghai–Xizang highways were opened to traffic.

西路军.n: Western Route Army of the Red Army
西路军.note: In late October 1936 three armies of the Red Fourth Front Army, more than 20,000 men, crossed the Yellow River westward at Jingyuan; in November they were named the Western Route Army and ordered to open a route to Xinjiang through the Hexi Corridor. They fought bloody battles against Ma Bufang's and Ma Buqing's forces at Gulang, Gaotai and Nijiayingzi and were defeated in March 1937; the remnants, more than 400 men led by Li Xiannian, reached Xingxingxia in April.

西里伯斯.note: Seat at Makassar; Manado in the north was a Christian area. From early 1942 a Japanese navy occupation zone. Reoccupied by the Netherlands after 1945; in December 1946 it became the core of the State of East Indonesia.

西里西亚.note: Cilicia, occupied by France after the First World War; in November 1919 the French also took over Marash, Aintab and Urfa from British troops, accompanied by the Armenian Legion. Marash and Urfa fell in turn in early 1920; under the Franco-Turkish Ankara Agreement of October 1921 the French troops withdrew in January 1922.

讨袁军.note:
The armies organized by KMT members to campaign against Yuan Shikai when Sun Yat-sen launched the Second Revolution in 1913.
After the assassination of Song Jiaoren and the Reorganization Loan, Yuan Shikai dismissed the KMT military governors of the three provinces of Jiangxi, Guangdong and Anhui. On 12 July Li Liejun was the first to take up arms, at Hukou in Jiangxi; Huang Xing held Nanjing, Bai Wenwei Anhui, Chen Qimei Shanghai and Chen Jiongming Guangdong, and Fujian, Hunan and Chongqing declared independence one after another.
The Beiyang Army advanced south along several routes, and within two months the provinces were defeated one after another; Nanjing fell on 1 September and Chongqing on the 12th, and Sun Yat-sen and Huang Xing went into exile in Japan.

谢苗诺夫.note:
Seat: Chita
The Cossack leader Semyonov entered and occupied Chita in September 1918 and, relying on Japanese troops and armoured trains, controlled the Transbaikal Railway; he was notorious for plunder and indiscriminate killing. Nominally he recognized Kolchak as Supreme Ruler from May 1919, and in January 1920 he was appointed to inherit Kolchak's authority in the Far East, renaming his domain the “Russian Eastern Outskirts”; in reality it was a White Guard separatist force backed by Japanese imperialism. In July 1920 Japan and the Far Eastern Republic agreed a ceasefire at Gongota; in October the Japanese troops withdrew from Transbaikalia, the People's Revolutionary Army stormed into Chita, Semyonov fled, and his remaining forces retreated into Northeast China.

谭延闿.note: Tan Yankai governed Hunan three times and was driven out by Zhao Hengti in November 1920. In 1923 Sun Yat-sen made him civil governor of Hunan and commander-in-chief of the Hunan Anti-Rebel Army; he broke into Changsha in August but was soon driven back by Zhao Hengti and Wu Peifu's reinforcements. He led his troops into Guangdong to hold the Bei River area, and in 1925 they were reorganized as the Second Army of the National Revolutionary Army.

赣军政府.note: Jiujiang declared independence first, on 23 October 1911, setting up the Jiujiang Military Sub-Government; the New Army rose in Nanchang on 31 October and declared independence the next day. The military governorship changed hands several times; in 1912 Li Liejun returned to Jiangxi to take charge.

赵倜.note: A product of the Yi Army, Zhao Ti was military governor of Henan in 1914–1922, sitting on the fence between the Anhui and Zhili cliques. In the First Zhili–Fengtian War of 1922 he secretly sided with the Fengtian Clique; his brother Zhao Jie attacked Zhengzhou and was defeated by Feng Yuxiang. Zhao Ti left office in May, and Henan passed to the Zhili Clique.

越南国.note:
Capital: Sài Gòn (Bảo Đại usually resided at Đà Lạt)
Polity: French-backed “associated state” of the French Union, with Bảo Đại as head of state
On 8 March 1949 Bảo Đại and French President Auriol signed the Élysée Accords; Cochinchina was merged in June, and on 1 July the State of Vietnam was established, divided into the three regions of North, Central and South Vietnam. The French still controlled military and foreign affairs; Britain and the United States recognized it in February 1950.
