On 4 June 1954 France and Vietnam initialled the Treaty of Independence, and in July Ngô Đình Diệm formed a cabinet; the Geneva Accords assigned the area south of the 17th parallel to its jurisdiction, but the State of Vietnam's delegate voiced opposition.

越南帝国.note:
Capital: Huế
Polity: Japanese-backed puppet monarchy; Emperor Bảo Đại, Prime Minister Trần Trọng Kim
On 9 March 1945 the Japanese army staged a coup that removed the French colonial authorities; on the 11th, at Japan's instigation, Bảo Đại proclaimed the abrogation of the Franco-Vietnamese protectorate treaties and Vietnam's “independence”; in August the Japanese handed Cochinchina, Hà Nội and Hải Phòng over to it. In the Viet Minh's August Revolution Bảo Đại abdicated on 30 August, and the empire came to an end.

越南民主共和国.note:
Capital: Hà Nội (from December 1946 to October 1954 the central government was based in the mountain base area of Việt Bắc)
Polity: led by the League for the Independence of Vietnam (Viet Minh); President Hồ Chí Minh, with Võ Nguyên Giáp commanding the army
In August 1945 the Indochinese Communist Party led the Viet Minh in launching the August Revolution, and on 2 September Hồ Chí Minh read the Declaration of Independence in Ba Đình Square, Hà Nội. North of the 16th parallel the Japanese surrender was accepted by Chinese troops, and south of it by British troops, after which the French colonial army staged a comeback. In March 1946 it concluded the Preliminary Agreement with France; on 19 December the Vietnamese people's War of Resistance against France broke out in full, and the government withdrew to the Việt Bắc Base Area. In January 1950 the People's Republic of China and the Soviet Union recognized it in turn, and in October the Border Campaign opened up the China–Vietnam border. Its offensives in the Red River Delta in 1951 were checked, and it shifted operations to the Northwest and Laos; in May 1954 the Vietnam People's Army won a great victory in the Điện Biên Phủ Campaign, and in July the Geneva Conference restored peace in Indochina, the accords making the area north of the 17th parallel its regroupment zone; it took over Hà Nội in October.

迈索尔.note: A large South Indian princely state ruled by the Maharajas of the Wodeyar dynasty, with its capital at Mysore and the government at Bangalore; noted for enlightened government and industrial development. Joined India in August 1947.

远东共和国.note:
Capital: Verkhneudinsk (1920.04–10) → Chita (1920.10–1922.11)
Polity: nominally an independent multi-party parliamentary republic, in fact directed by the Far Eastern Bureau of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks); a buffer state between Soviet Russia and the Japanese troops stationed in Siberia
Proclaimed at Verkhneudinsk on 6 April 1920, it covered Transbaikalia, the Amur region, Primorye and Kamchatka. In October 1920 the People's Revolutionary Army pulled out Semyonov's “Chita cork”, and in February 1922 it drove back the Whites at Volochayevka; after the Japanese troops left Vladivostok in October, the republic was merged into the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic on 15 November.

邓本殷.note: A subordinate of Chen Jiongming who from 1923 held the eight prefectures of Gao, Lei, Qin, Lian, Qiong, Ya, Luo and Yang in southern Guangdong as the Eight Prefectures Allied Army, acting in concert with Chen Jiongming from afar and attaching himself to the Beiyang warlords. From October 1925 the Nationalist Government waged its Southern Campaign, taking Hainan early the following year, and Deng Benyin fled.

鄂军政府.note: The Hubei Military Governorate of the Military Government of the Republic of China, established at Wuchang on 11 October 1911 with the brigade commander Li Yuanhong chosen as military governor. It was the first to send circular telegrams to the provinces, under the name “Republic of China”, calling for the overthrow of Qing rule. In the Battle of Yangxia it lost Hankou and Hanyang but held Wuchang until the ceasefire and peace talks.

鄂西靖国军.note: In December 1917 Shi Xingchuan at Jingzhou and Li Tiancai at Xiangyang declared independence in response to the Constitution Protection Movement, but were soon defeated by the Beiyang Army; the remnants, with Tang Keming, Cai Jimin and others, held the Shinan (Enshi) area as the Western Hubei National Pacification Army, linking up with the Constitution Protection armies of Sichuan and Hunan. After 1919 they were gradually absorbed or broke up.

鄂豫皖苏区.note: Formed in the Dabie Mountains after the Huangma Uprising of 1927 and the Shangnan and Liu-Huo uprisings of 1929, with Xinji as its capital. In November 1931 the Red Fourth Front Army was formed and fought four campaigns in succession at Huang'an, Shang-Huang, Sujiabu and Huang-Guang; at its height the area covered more than twenty counties. After defeat in the fourth counter-“encirclement” campaign in 1932 the main force moved west to Sichuan and Shaanxi, and the troops left behind held out until the Long March of the Red 25th Army in 1934.

鄂豫边区.note: The anti-Japanese base area opened up by the New Fourth Army's 5th Division (Li Xiannian), centred on Jingshan, Anlu and Mount Dawu in Hubei and straddling the borders of the five provinces of Hubei, Henan, Anhui, Hunan and Jiangxi. It grew out of the Henan-Hubei Independent Guerrilla Detachment of 1939; in April 1941 the Henan-Hubei Border Region Joint Military-Administrative Office was set up, later reorganized as an administrative office. Wedged between the Beiping–Hankou Railway, the Han River and the KMT's Fifth War Zone, it expanded at the end of the War of Resistance into southern Henan, eastern Hubei and northern Hunan, and was the westernmost CPC anti-Japanese base area in Central China.

鄂豫陕根据地.note: The Red 25th Army (Wu Huanxian, Xu Haidong, Cheng Zihua) left Hubei-Henan-Anhui on its Long March in November 1934 and in December established a base area around Yujiahe in the Shangluo mountains, spanning Shangxian, Luonan, Shanyang, Yunxi and Lushi. In July 1935 it moved west and north, reached northern Shaanxi in September, and was merged with the northern Shaanxi Red Army into the Red Fifteenth Army Group.

金马.n: Kinmen, Matsu and other islands (held by KMT forces)
金马.note: After the liberation of Xiamen in October 1949, the remnants of Tang Enbo's forces and Hu Lian's 12th Army Group held Kinmen. In the Battle of Kinmen on 25–27 October, the more than 9,000 PLA troops who had landed on the island were all killed or captured; Kinmen, together with Matsu, Dachen and other islands, thus long remained occupied by KMT forces, becoming the front line of the confrontation across the Taiwan Strait. In the early 1950s the KMT forces still held Kinmen, Matsu and Wuqiu off the Fujian–Zhejiang coast and the Dachen, Yijiangshan, Yushan, Pishan and Nanji islands of Zhejiang, harassing the mainland coast with guerrilla units; they attacked Nanri Island in October 1952 and Dongshan Island in July 1953. On 3 September 1954 the PLA shelled Kinmen, and the First Taiwan Strait Crisis broke out. (The Dachen, Yijiangshan and other islands are too small to appear as land on the base map, so no map points were set on them; Yijiangshan Island was liberated in January 1955 and the KMT forces withdrew from Dachen and Nanji in February, after the period of this map.)

锡兰.note:
Capital: Colombo
Polity: British Crown colony from 1802, ruled by a governor; the Donoughmore Constitution of 1931 introduced universal adult suffrage and a State Council; a dominion within the Commonwealth from 4 February 1948
Key figures: Senanayake (first prime minister)
Key events: in the Second World War it was the base of the British Eastern Fleet and South East Asia Command (the latter moving to Kandy in 1944), and in April 1942 it was attacked from the air by the Japanese carrier fleet.

锡金.note: A small Himalayan state under the hereditary rule of the Chogyal; after the Qing government was forced to sign the Sino-British Convention relating to Sikkim and Xizang in 1890 it became a British protectorate, with a Political Officer at Gangtok; it commanded the trade route into Xizang via Yadong. After 1947 it maintained the status quo with India, and in December 1950 it became an Indian protectorate.

镇嵩军.note: A local army formed by the Beiyang warlord Liu Zhenhua from irregular troops around Songxian in western Henan, garrisoning western Henan in the early Republic; in 1918 Liu Zhenhua became concurrently civil governor of Shaanxi, and the Zhensong Army occupied Guanzhong, returning to western Henan in 1925. In 1926, attached to Wu Peifu, it besieged Xi'an, held by Yang Hucheng and Li Huchen, for eight months from April; tens of thousands starved to death in the city. On 28 November the Guominjun Allied Army lifted the siege, the Zhensong Army fell back to western Henan, and in spring 1927 it went over to Feng Yuxiang.

闽军政府.note: The New Army rose in Fuzhou on 9 November 1911; after fierce fighting at Yushan the Banner garrison surrendered, and the brigade commander Sun Daoren became military governor. During the Second Revolution Fujian briefly declared independence but soon revoked it; Sun Daoren left office at the end of that year.

闽浙赣苏区.note: The northeastern Jiangxi base area opened up by Fang Zhimin and Shao Shiping after the Yi-Heng Uprising of 1928, centred on Geyuan in Hengfeng; the Red Tenth Army was formed in 1930, and in December 1932 the area was renamed Fujian-Zhejiang-Jiangxi Province, governing more than twenty counties in northeastern Jiangxi, northern Fujian and southwestern Zhejiang. In January 1935 the northward march of the Red Tenth Army Group failed, and Fang Zhimin was captured and heroically met his martyrdom.

阿塞拜疆.note:
Capital: Ganja, moved to Baku in September 1918
Polity: democratic republic established on 28 May 1918, governed by the Musavat party; the first republic in the Muslim world
Key events: took Baku in September 1918 with the help of the Ottoman “Army of Islam”; contested Karabakh, Zangezur and Nakhichevan with Armenia; the Red Army entered Baku on 28 April 1920 and the country was Sovietized; the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast was set up in 1923 and the Nakhichevan Autonomous Republic in 1924.

阿塞拜疆人民政府.note:
Capital: Tabriz
Polity: Soviet-backed autonomous government, ruled by the Azerbaijan Democratic Party
Key figures: Jafar Pishevari
Key events: rose in the Soviet occupation zone from November 1945 and was proclaimed on 12 December; after the Soviet withdrawal in May 1946 it negotiated with Tehran; in December Iranian troops entered Tabriz, the regime collapsed and Pishevari fled to the Soviet Union.

阿富汗.note:
Capital: Kabul
Polity: monarchy of the Barakzai dynasty; Emir Habibullah (1901–1919), Amanullah (1919–1929, styled king from 1926), Nadir Shah (1929–1933), Zahir Shah (from 1933)
Key events: forced to sign the Treaty of Gandamak in 1879, after which its foreign relations were under British control; in 1919 Amanullah declared full independence, which after the Third Anglo-Afghan War was confirmed by the Treaty of Rawalpindi in August; his reforms provoked rebellion, Kalakani took Kabul in January 1929, and Nadir Khan retook it in October; neutral in the Second World War.

阿尔泰区.note: Jurisdiction of the Altay Amban, separated from Kobdo in 1906, with its seat at Chenghuasi (present-day Altay, Xinjiang). Early in the Republic it was placed under an Altay Administrator directly subordinate to the Beijing Government; reinforcements from Xinjiang and Gansu held off Outer Mongolian forces here. Merged into Xinjiang in 1919.

阿拉斯加.note: Purchased by the United States from Russia in 1867 and organized as a territory in 1912. Attu and Kiska in the western Aleutians, facing Kamchatka across the sea, were occupied by Japanese troops in June 1942, the only US territory in North America occupied by enemy forces in the Second World War; they were recovered in summer 1943.

阿拉维.note: In 1920 France set up the Alawite Territory centred on Latakia; it became the Alawite State in 1922 and was called the Government of Latakia from 1930; it was merged into Syria in December 1936 (separated again for a time in 1939–1942).

阿曼.note:
Capital: Muscat
Polity: sultanate of the Al Said dynasty, bound to Britain by treaty and under its influence; it also held Gwadar on the Baluch coast and Dhofar in the south
Key figures: Sultans Faisal, Taimur and Said bin Taimur (from 1932)
Key events: in 1913 the Ibadis of the interior elected a rival imam, whose forces attacked Muscat in January 1915 and were driven off by British Indian troops; under the Treaty of Seeb of September 1920 the sultan recognized the interior's autonomy; from 1952 it disputed the Buraimi Oasis with Saudi Arabia, and from 1954 it sent troops towards Fahud to prospect for oil in the interior.

阿曼伊玛目.note:
Capital: Nizwa
Polity: imamate whose imams were elected by the Ibadis
Key figures: Imams Salim al-Kharusi (1913–1920), Muhammad al-Khalili (1920–1954), Ghalib al-Hinai (from 1954)
Key events: rose against the Sultan of Muscat in May 1913; the British-mediated Treaty of Seeb of September 1920 gave the interior de facto autonomy; on al-Khalili's death in 1954 Ghalib succeeded him and, with Saudi support, sharpened the confrontation with the sultan; the sultan's troops entered Nizwa in December 1955, and the imamate was put down after the Jebel Akhdar War of 1957–1959.

阿萨姆.note: Capital at Shillong. Re-established as a chief commissioner's province in 1912 and made a governor's province in 1921. Home to tea gardens and the Digboi oilfield; in 1942–1945 it was the starting point of the Hump route and the China–India Road carrying aid to China, and in 1944 Japanese troops attacked Imphal and Kohima. In 1947 Sylhet voted by referendum to join East Pakistan.

阿西尔.note:
Capital: Sabya
Polity: Sufi emirate founded by the Idrisi family, holding the Red Sea coastal lowlands
Key figures: Muhammad al-Idrisi (1909–1923)
Key events: rose against the Ottomans in 1910, received Italian aid during the Italo-Turkish War and allied with Britain in the First World War; took over Hodeidah from British forces in 1921, but Yemen took it back in 1925; became a Saudi protectorate under the Mecca Agreement of October 1926 and was annexed by the Saudis in 1930; a revolt in 1932–1933 failed.

陕军.note: General name for the provincial armies of Republican Shaanxi. In 1916 Chen Shufan drove out Lu Jianzhang and became military governor of Shaanxi, attaching himself to the Anhui Clique and locked in a stalemate with the Shaanxi National Pacification Army; in 1921 he was driven out by Yan Xiangwen and Feng Yuxiang of the Zhili Clique. Thereafter Shaanxi was controlled in turn by the Zhensong Army and the Second and Third Armies of the Guominjun, while Yang Hucheng, who came from the National Pacification Army, built up his strength moving between northern Shaanxi and the area north of the Wei River. In 1926 Yang Hucheng and Li Huchen held Xi'an for eight months; in 1930 Yang Hucheng led the 17th Route Army into Shaanxi and became provincial chairman, and the Shaanxi Army thereafter meant the 17th Route Army. In 1936 Yang Hucheng and Zhang Xueliang launched the Xi'an Incident; after its peaceful settlement Yang Hucheng was forced to go abroad, and his troops were reorganized into the 38th Army and other units.

陕军政府.note: On 22 October 1911 the New Army and the Gelaohui rose in Xi'an, stormed the Manchu quarter and chose Zhang Fenghui as Grand Commander. It held off the Henan Yi Army at Tong Pass to the east and Shengyun's Gansu army at Qianzhou to the west, fighting hard until the abdication of the Qing emperor.

陕甘宁.note: The Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Soviet Area was renamed the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region on 6 September 1937, nominally a special region under the Nationalist Government, with its capital at Yan'an and Lin Boqu as chairman. It governed more than twenty counties in northern Shaanxi, eastern Gansu and southeastern Ningxia, with a population of about 1.5 million, and was the seat of the CPC Central Committee and the main rear base of the Eighth Route Army. Hu Zongnan's forces occupied Yan'an in March 1947, and the Northwest People's Liberation Army recovered it in April 1948; the Border Region was abolished in January 1950.

陕甘苏区.note: Founded by Liu Zhidan, Xie Zichang and Xi Zhongxun. After the Zhaojin Soviet Area was lost in 1933, the Shaanxi-Gansu Border Soviet Government was set up at Nanliang in Huachi in November 1934, while in northern Shaanxi there was a separate guerrilla zone around Anding; in spring and summer 1935 six counties were taken in succession, and the two areas were joined into the Northwest Revolutionary Base Area. The Red 25th Army arrived in September of that year and the Central Red Army in October; after the Western Expedition of 1936 it was called the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Soviet Area, becoming the destination of the Long March of the Party Central Committee and the Red Army and the starting point from which the Eighth Route Army set out for the anti-Japanese front.

陕西靖国军.note: In January 1918 Guo Jian, Hu Jingyi and others rose in Shaanxi in response to the Constitution Protection Movement; in August Yu Youren returned to Shaanxi as commander-in-chief. Holding Sanyuan and Fuping north of the Wei River, the National Pacification Army fought Chen Shufan, the Zhensong Army and Xu Lanzhou's forces of the Fengtian Army to a stalemate for three years. In 1921 Hu Jingyi accepted reorganization by the Zhili Clique, and Yang Hucheng's forces moved into northern Shaanxi.

青马.note: The Ma family army of Hehuang, based at Xining. Ma Qi was Garrison Commissioner of Ninghai on the Gansu frontier from 1915 and held real power over provincial affairs after Qinghai became a province in 1929; after his death in 1931 the uncle and nephew Ma Lin and Ma Bufang succeeded in turn. In 1938 Ma Bufang became chairman of Qinghai and his troops were expanded into the 82nd Army; he ruled Qinghai until 1949.

革命军.note:
Collective name for the military governments (military governorates) set up one after another in the provinces after the Wuchang Uprising of October 1911, under the name “Republic of China”.
On 29 December delegates of the provincial military governors meeting in Nanjing elected Sun Yat-sen provisional president, and on 1 January 1912 the Provisional Government of the Republic of China was established, a regime of a bourgeois-republican nature; Huang Xing was minister of the army, and the Senate drew up the Provisional Constitution.
In February the Qing emperor abdicated, Sun Yat-sen was forced to resign, and the Senate elected Yuan Shikai to succeed him: the fruits of the 1911 Revolution were usurped by Yuan Shikai. In April the Provisional Government moved north, and the provincial military governments became Republican military governorates.

韩复榘.note: Han Fuju was originally a subordinate of Feng Yuxiang; in May 1929 he and Shi Yousan changed sides and went over to Chiang, and he became chairman of Henan. He helped Chiang in the Central Plains War, became chairman of Shandong in September 1930, drove Liu Zhennian out of Jiaodong in 1932 and took sole control of the whole province, nominally under Nanjing but forming his own faction. At the end of 1937 he abandoned Shandong without a fight, and in January of the following year he was executed by the Nationalist Government.

香港.note: In 1842 the Qing government was forced to sign the Treaty of Nanjing, ceding Hong Kong Island; the Convention of Beijing of 1860 ceded the southern tip of the Kowloon Peninsula, and in 1898 Britain forcibly leased the New Territories for 99 years. Britain's entrepôt and naval base in the Far East. In 1925–1926 the CPC led the Guangzhou–Hong Kong Strike; on 25 December 1941 Governor Young surrendered to the Japanese army, and Hong Kong remained under Japanese occupation for three years and eight months until British forces returned on 30 August 1945.

马仲英部.note: Ma Zhongying's Hui army from Hezhou, Gansu, given the designation New 36th Division by Nanjing. From 1931 it twice entered Xinjiang at the invitation of the Hami rebels, and in 1933–1934 twice besieged Dihua; defeated by Sheng Shicai with the help of Soviet troops, it went south to Kashi and crushed the “East Turkestan” separatist regime there. In July 1934 Ma Zhongying went into the Soviet Union, and his troops, led by Ma Hushan, held the Hotan area until 1937.

马哈巴德.note:
Capital: Mahabad
Polity: Kurdish republic, ruled by the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran
Key figures: Qazi Muhammad (president), Mustafa Barzani
Key events: proclaimed on 22 January 1946 and dependent on Soviet support, it held a corner south of Lake Urmia; Iranian troops occupied it in December, Qazi Muhammad was executed the following March, and Barzani fought his way with his men into the Soviet Union.

马尔代夫.note: The Sultanate of the Maldives, a British protectorate from 1887, its external affairs handled by the Governor of Ceylon. Its first written constitution was promulgated in 1932; after Ceylon's independence in 1948 it concluded a separate protection agreement with Britain.

马德拉斯.note: Capital at Madras; it covered both coasts of South India and the southern Deccan. It saw the Moplah Rebellion in Malabar in 1921 and the rise of the Justice Party and the non-Brahmin movement. Ganjam and other areas were transferred to Orissa in 1936. It went to India in 1947.

马来亚.note: In April 1946 Britain combined the Federated Malay States, the Unfederated Malay States, Penang and Malacca into the Malayan Union; the sultans surrendered their sovereignty, provoking fierce Malay opposition. In February 1948 it was reorganized as the Federation of Malaya, restoring the sultans' position. In June that year the Malayan Communist Party led an armed struggle against British rule, and the British colonial authorities declared an “Emergency”. In October 1951 the High Commissioner, Gurney, was killed in an ambush; Templer arrived the following year and forcibly pushed through the “New Villages” scheme and the “hearts and minds” policy, and the MCP's armed struggle ran into difficulties.

马来属邦.note: Johore, together with Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Trengganu, which were transferred from Siam in 1909; the sultans of these states kept more autonomy, Britain sending only Advisers. In 1943 Japan assigned the four northern states to Thailand; they were returned in 1945 and merged into the Malayan Union in 1946.

马来联邦.note: The four protected states of Perak, Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang, federated in 1895 with the capital at Kuala Lumpur; British Residents controlled the administration, and tin mining and rubber planting flourished. Occupied by Japanese troops in January 1942; merged into the Malayan Union in April 1946.

驻藏川军.note: The Sichuan Army troops that entered Xizang with Zhong Ying in 1910, stationed at Lhasa, Gyangze, Xigaze and Yadong. They mutinied after the Wuchang Uprising, and the Amban in Xizang, Lianyu, lost his authority; in 1912 the upper strata of Xizang launched the “expulsion of the Han”, and the Sichuan troops fought the Tibetan army and were disarmed under two ceasefire agreements. In December of that year Zhong Ying led the remnants out of Lhasa, most of them returning to the interior by way of India.

高加索.note: The Russian Caucasus Viceroyalty, seated at Tiflis, covering the Transcaucasian governorates and the Kars and Batum oblasts taken from the Ottomans in 1878. After the February Revolution of 1917 it was replaced by the Special Transcaucasian Committee, and in 1918 it split into the three states of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

高尔察克政府.note:
Capital: Omsk (moved east to Irkutsk in November 1919)
Polity: counter-revolutionary military dictatorship, with Admiral Kolchak as “Supreme Ruler of Russia”; the Allied powers, intervening militarily against Soviet Russia, supplied it with arms and advisers
In May 1918 the Czechoslovak Legion revolted along the Trans-Siberian Railway and the local Soviet governments were overthrown one after another; Omsk became the seat first of the Provisional Siberian Government and then of the Ufa Directory (which moved there from Ufa in October); on 18 November Kolchak seized sole power in a coup, and Denikin's and other White armies in southern Russia nominally accepted his command. In spring 1919 his forces pushed west to near the Volga River before being driven back by the Red Army; he lost the Urals in July and Omsk in November; after the Irkutsk Uprising of January 1920 Kolchak was handed over by the Czechoslovak Legion and was executed on 7 February.

鲁苏战区.n: Shandong-Jiangsu War Zone (Yu Xuezhong, Han Deqin)
鲁苏战区.note: Set up in 1939 with Yu Xuezhong as commander-in-chief, who held the Yimeng Mountains with former Northeastern Army troops; Han Deqin, deputy commander-in-chief and chairman of Jiangsu Province, held Xinghua and Dongtai, and Li Mingyang's forces at Taizhou were also under it. Isolated behind enemy lines, it fought the Japanese and puppet forces but also repeatedly clashed with the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army, and Han Deqin's forces attacked the New Fourth Army many times. In 1941 Li Changjiang went over to the enemy at Taizhou; in early 1943 Wu Huawen went over to the enemy and Han Deqin was defeated; in August Yu Xuezhong's forces withdrew to northern Anhui, and the war zone existed in name only.

黎巴嫩.note:
Capital: Beirut
Polity: on 1 September 1920 France created “Greater Lebanon”, adding the Beqaa Valley, Tripoli, Tyre and other areas; it became a republic in 1926, with power apportioned among religious communities
Key events: in November 1943 the Free French authorities arrested President Khoury and others for amending the constitution, provoking nationwide protests; they were released on the 22nd, which became Independence Day; in the same year the National Pact laid down that the president would be a Maronite and the prime minister a Sunni; the last French troops left in December 1946; joined the war against Israel in 1948.

黔军.note: The provincial army of Republican Guizhou. In the National Protection and Constitution Protection periods it was led by Liu Xianshi and Wang Wenhua of the Xingyi faction, belonging to the southwestern Constitution Protection camp. In the Minguo 9 Incident of November 1920 Wang Wenhua's faction drove out Liu Xianshi; the next year Wang Wenhua was assassinated in Shanghai, and Lu Tao took charge. In 1922 Yuan Zuming returned to Guizhou with Wu Peifu's help, but soon went off to fight in Sichuan; in 1923–1925 the Yunnan Army entered Guiyang and propped up Liu Xianshi. In 1926 the forces of Yuan Zuming, Peng Hanzhang, Wang Tianpei and others were incorporated into the National Revolutionary Army, and Zhou Xicheng governed Guizhou; Zhou Xicheng was killed in battle in 1929, and Mao Guangxiang and Wang Jialie governed in turn. In 1935 the KMT Central Army entered Guizhou in pursuit of the Red Army, and the Guizhou Army was reorganized.

黔军政府.note: Established after the uprising of the New Army and the Self-Government Society in Guiyang on 4 November 1911, with Yang Jincheng as military governor. In March 1912 the Constitutional Faction (constitutionalists) brought Tang Jiyao's Yunnan Army into Guizhou; it occupied Guiyang, and the revolutionaries of the Self-Government Society were suppressed.

龙济光.note: Long Jiguang came from a native-chieftain family of Mengzi, Yunnan, and commanded the Ji Army stationed in Guangxi and Guangdong. In August 1913, on Yuan Shikai's orders, he seized Guangzhou and became military governor of Guangdong, brutally suppressing KMT members. On 6 April 1916 he was forced to declare independence, but in fact remained hostile to the National Protection Army.
